abstracts:
{'cdata!': "The development objective of the
            Additional Financing for the Bihar Rural Livelihood Project
            is to enhance social and economic empowerment of the rural
            poor in Bihar. The Additional Financing (AF) will scale up
            the project's impact and effectiveness through: 1)
            federating and building the capacity of the women managed
            community based organizations at village and block level, 2)
            convergence with various ongoing schemes and programs of the
            Government of India/Government of Bihar (GOI/GOB) in the
            areas of health and nutrition, social protection, rural
            employment, agriculture through demand side interventions
            and strengthening the last mile service delivery mechanisms,
            3) enhance financial and economic inclusion and
            capitalization of the poor through collaborative frameworks
            with a variety of private, civil society, and social
            enterprise partner organizations, and 4) strengthen the
            Monitoring and Evaluation (M&E) system to capture
            changes in social and economic empowerment in household
            economy and behavior. The AF is consistent with the
            development objective of the ongoing Bihar Rural Livelihoods Project."}

abstracts:
{'cdata!': "The objective of the Punjab State Road
            Sector Project for India is to improve operating conditions
            of State roads for road users, in a sustainable way, thus
            helping to provide the business enabling environment
            necessary to support Punjab's economic development
            strategy. This paper extends the loan closing date by five
            years until June 5, 2017, from the original closing date of
            June 5, 2012. The reason for seeking the five year extension
            is to support Government of Punjab (GOP) in their endeavor
            to undertake a 10 year network based Output and Performance
            Based Road Contract (OPRC) to improve, rehabilitate and
            maintain about 200 km of state road network as part of road
            upgrading, rehabilitation and maintenance component. This
            network based demonstration project, based on asset
            management principles is being implemented for the first
            time in India and has the potential of being replicated
            elsewhere in the country. The restructuring includes changes
            to: (i) results monitoring framework; (ii) scope of project
            components; (iii) applicability of January 2011 version of
            procurement guidelines and consultant guidelines; (iv)
            changes in project costs and;(v) corresponding changes to
            legal amendments including dropping of covenants related to
            Road Maintenance Fund."}

abstracts:
{'cdata!': 'The Punjab State Road Sector Project for
            India aims at increasing the service levels of the state
            roads. This restructuring is for an interim extension of the
            loan closing date for the project for three months from the
            current loan closing date of June 5, 2012 until September 5,
            2012. This interim extension is required to prepare and
            submit a detailed case for extension of the loan closing
            date for five year to support a new long-term asset
            management for the road network. The five extension request
            would entail a first level project restructuring, The
            Government of Punjab has recommended a 5 year loan
            extension, duly endorsed by Department of Economic Affairs.
            Second phase Output and Performance-based Road Contracts
            (OPRC) contract, which is a ten year long contract on asset
            management principles, requires technical support and
            handholding of the Government for at least the first five
            years. The Government of Punjab at several occasions
            indicated their commitment towards this project and the new
            long-term asset management concept.'}

abstracts:
{'cdata!': 'Road improvement works for the Punjab
            State Road Sector Project for India are likely to have
            adverse social impacts. Acquisition of land, eviction of
            squatters and encroachers are also likely to cause social
            disruption and economic loss for Project Affected Persons
            and their families. This plan aims to minimize disturbance
            and loss to affected populations because of the project. In
            keeping with this aim, a Base Line Socio-Economic Survey was
            conducted to identify the affected persons due to the
            widening of the road, determine the effect of the project on
            the people and community, explore options for minimizing the
            adverse effects, and also to come up with a Resettlement and
            Rehabilitation Action Plan that will ensure restoration of
            livelihoods. This document provides details about the
            Project Affected Families and appropriate resettlement
            mechanisms to be used, as well as various activities during
            project implementation that will minimize adverse social
            impacts on the people and the area. Under the resettlement
            policy and relevant laws, there is provision to pay
            resettlement assistance to displaced persons including the
            non-title holders for loss of structures, additional
            assistance for those belonging to vulnerable categories and
            provision for negotiating compensation for land and property
            lost on the basis of replacement cost. Apart from this, all
            payments (compensation and resettlement and rehabilitation
            assistance) will be made to affected persons before taking
            over possession of such land. Transitional allowance,
            shifting allowance, skill up-grading/training for affected
            people, assistance for damage to standing crops, the choice
            for resettling either in the resettlement colony or
            self-relocation, etc., have been included to ensure
            restoration of livelihood within a reasonable period of time.'}

            and operational performance of selected existing dams in the

            project implementation immediately after effectiveness of

abstracts:
{'cdata!': "This environmental assessment for
            India's Second Uttar Pradesh Agricultural
            Diversification Project assesses environmental impacts and
            possible environmental and social risks in activities aiming
            to increase areas and yields of diversified field and tree
            crop, livestock, and fish products, and increase the
            proportion marketed and processed. It proposes good
            environmental practices to integrate into project activities
            to promote sustainable natural resource management. A long
            list of environmental concerns and risks include using a
            poor quality of bio-pesticides and increasing level of
            fertilizer and pesticide use generally, poor storage and
            handling of seeds that are themselves of poor quality,
            decline in crop yields and loss of soil fertility, increased
            use of bio-agents, higher demand for irrigation water for
            vegetables and increased water demand, more electricity
            consumption and disposal of polyethylene sheets, waste
            generation at source causing water pollution, methane gas
            generation, intercropping leading to increased chemical use
            to control pests, introduction of genetically modified
            varieties, crates adding to pollution, methane emissions,
            milk contamination, exotic species intrusion and fish
            contamination, and construction debris. Among the mitigation
            measures recommended are: Strictly monitor the quality of
            bio-pesticides. Use action plan to store and handle seeds.
            Create database of seed certifying agencies, simplify seed
            certification process, and involve nongovernmental
            organizations in seed testing. Test pH of farmers'
            soil. Convert to bio-fertilizers and bio-pesticides. Apply
            improved technology to composting and water saving and
            harvesting for certain crops. Keep crop output in cold
            storage, improve marketing system, and use sprinkler
            irrigation for horticultural crops. Install biogas plants to
            reuse plant waste and use disposal system for other solid
            waste and wastewater. Train farmers on integrated pest
            management, agro-biodiversity, soil drainage, and labeling
            and certification. Promote the use of biodegradable crates
            and their safe disposal, and hazardous waste disposal,
            including poultry droppings. The report addresses social
            risks by recommending that farmers actively participate to
            combat mistrust about pest control methods, making the
            community environmentally aware and using farmer-friendly
            project methods, training field staff and farmers to
            facilitate technology transfer technology and increase
            economic output, and promoting cost effective production
            certification and labeling in organic and contract farming."}

abstracts:
{'cdata!': 'The objective of the Biodiversity
            Conservation and Rural Livelihoods Improvement Project for
            India is to develop and promote new models of conservation
            at the landscape scale through enhanced capacity and
            institution building for mainstreaming biodiversity
            conservation outcomes. There are four components to the
            project. The first component of the project is
            demonstration of landscape conservation approaches in two
            pilot sites: this component will develop tools, techniques,
            knowledge and skills towards improved conservation and rural
            livelihoods outcomes in the little Rann of Kutch in Gujarat
            and Askot in Uttarakhand; the second component to the
            project is to strengthening knowledge management and
            national capacity for landscape conservation: this component
            will support improved knowledge and capacity building on
            learning and experience from the two demonstration
            landscapes and other local conservation models; the third
            component of the project is to scaling up and replication of
            successful models of conservation in additional landscape
            sites: this component would support the further testing and
            replication of landscape conservation approaches to two
            additional high biodiversity landscapes from the third year
            onwards with project financing; and the fourth component of
            the project is to national coordination for landscape
            conservation: this component will support coordination for
            landscape conservation at the Ministry of Environment and
            Forests (MOEF).'}

abstracts:
{'cdata!': "Ratings for the Third Power System
            Development (PSDP III) Project for India were as follows:
            outcomes were highly satisfactory, the risk to development
            outcome was low or negligible, the Bank performance was
            satisfactory, and the Borrower performance was also
            satisfactory. Some lessons learned included: impact of
            compliance with the negative pledge clause: This process
            required a careful and lengthy preparation of the security
            package by Power Grid Corporation of India Limited
            (POWERGRID) which delayed loan effectiveness by about six
            months (July 31 to December 15, 2006). It would have been
            useful to resolve this aspect earlier during preparation so
            that implementation could proceed according to the planned
            timeline. This is a broader lesson for the India portfolio.
            However, the resolution of this issue and experience gained
            during the approval process resulted in the streamlining of
            the approval of PSDP IV and V by the World Bank. Using
            operational and project management experience, POWERGRID has
            effectively contributed to the success of the project.
            Moreover, this project has shown that continuous reviews and
            improvements of POWERGRID's technical implementation,
            procurement and safeguards systems have elevated the
            standards to be followed by others. Procurement is a
            delicate matter and with its overlapping synergies with the
            technical aspects, it is always a tough and contentious
            issue. Thus, even though there was a regular communication
            (both formal and informal) between POWERGRID and the Bank
            during the entire project period, an additional exchange
            forum, which could be in the form of regular face-to-face
            meetings, between the Bank and POWERGRID to discuss such
            complex matters in even more detail shall help in future engagements."}

abstracts:
{'cdata!': 'This environmental and social assessment
            for the Third Power System Development Project for India
            outlines possible negative impacts and proposes measures to
            mitigate them. Expected negative environmental impacts can
            be mitigated as follows: Avoid affecting natural and
            socio-cultural resources by carefully selecting routes using
            techniques/tools like GIS and GPS aerial photography. Obtain
            prior approval and have forestry department supervise when
            passing transmission lines through forest and protected
            areas. Provide construction crews with fuel wood or
            alternative fuels to minimize fuel collecting. Pay
            compensation for crop damage or other damage to farmland,
            and restore on-farm works after construction ends. Reroute
            telecom circuits, convert overhead telecom circuits into
            cables, etc. to minimize voltage interference. Maintain
            adequate clearance between transmission lines and railways,
            civil aviation, and defense installations. Paint airport
            towers beyond specified height for easy visibility and place
            warning lights on top of these towers. Where drainage is
            affected, train flow and guide it to safe zones. Adopt
            safety measures to avoid fires due to flashover from lines.
            Resurface the areas where excavation works are done. Restore
            surfaces with topsoil. Select dumping areas to for rocky
            material and use as fill for tower foundations. Plant trees
            along roads to buffer visual effect. Paint towers to blend
            into background. Provide sound and vibration dampers, and
            maintain equipment to reduce noise. Reduce nuisance to
            nearby properties by using tractors and manual labor.
            Execute work during light traffic periods. Avoid rainy
            season, cut and fill slopes, use retaining walls, and sow
            soil-binding grasses to control erosion. Protect worker
            health and safety. There are no significant issues regarding
            management of levels of polychlorinated biphenyls PCBs)
            formerly used as insulating material in capacitors and transformers.'}

{'cdata!': 'This resettlement action plan presents

abstracts:
{'cdata!': "Following two decades of relatively
            rapid growth, and a decade of liberalization, there is
            growing confidence within India, as well as internationally,
            about the state of the economy, and India's development
            potential. Nonetheless, and particularly since the late
            nineties, when India's states experienced a sharp
            fiscal deterioration, they have faced a squeeze on
            development spending, particularly acute in the poorer ones.
            In response, most state governments embarked on fiscal
            reforms, aimed at reducing deficits, and enabling effective
            interventions in priority areas. States in India play an
            increasingly important role in devising, and implementing
            policies to stimulate economic growth, and promote human
            development. But the performance of India's states is
            increasingly divergent, State deficits and debt levels rose
            sharply in the late nineties, and off-budget liabilities
            also increased rapidly. This sharp fiscal deterioration gave
            rise to state-level fiscal adjustment efforts, which in
            recent years have shown some signs of improved fiscal
            performance. Concerns about the level, and composition of
            fiscal deficits remain. The report states that a halt in
            reforms would endanger the states quality and quantity of
            productive expenditures, while debt levels would steadily
            build. It reviews expenditure reforms - particularly
            salaries, at the core of expenditure restructuring - and,
            pensions as a rapidly-mounting liability, which can be
            contained by parametric reforms, and longer-term structural
            reforms, while also examines subsidies, exemplifying the
            difficulties involved in reforming subsidy regimes.
            Regarding power sector reforms, commercial discipline should
            be a top priority. Public enterprise reforms are outlined,
            suggesting that while immediate fiscal gains may not be
            achieved, such reforms will prevent future budgetary support
            from keeping loss-making enterprises afloat. On examining
            revenue reforms, the report indicates these are essential to
            reduce fiscal imbalances, suggesting the elimination of tax
            on inter-state exports is critical, and should proceed with,
            or without the value-added tax (VAT), specifying tax
            administration reforms are perhaps more important than tax
            reforms. On strengthening the fiscal federal framework, it
            is recommended States need more flexibility to borrow, but
            under a centrally-imposed aggregate borrowing cap. Three
            institutional reform would therefore help fiscal federalism
            in India: Finance Commission as a permanent body; entrusting
            a single agency in compiling timely state-level fiscal data;
            and, reviewing the role of the Planning Commission."}

abstracts:
{'cdata!': 'Agriculture in India will remain the
            mainstay for a large share of the rural population in the
            next decade, many of which also comprise the rural poor.
            Promoting more rapid agricultural growth, particularly
            achieving the government goal of 4 percent growth per year
            not only exclusively during the 10th plan period but for the
            medium to longer term, will be extremely crucial not only to
            achieving strong economic performance for the country as a
            whole, but also in lifting large numbers of agricultural
            households above poverty. The reform agenda puts in the
            spotlight the difficult challenge of balancing short vs.
            longer term policies and expenditure priorities to achieve
            targets. The current subsidy-dominated agricultural
            environment is helping to keep farming many crops viable and
            even highly lucrative, especially food grain crops in
            traditional procurement states. But in distorting farmer
            incentives, it is eroding rapidly the basic foundation for
            agriculture (i.e. that is, land and water resources),
            threatening the longer-term viability of agricultural
            production, and thus would also diminish future growth
            prospects and risk increasing rural poverty in many of these
            areas. Action to regain a better balance between short and
            longer-term policy and expenditure priorities to ensure
            sustainable poverty reducing agricultural growth can no
            longer be postponed.'}

{'cdata!': "Ratings for the Carbon Tetrachloride

abstracts:
{'cdata!': 'Carbon tetrachloride (CTC) is an ozone
            depleting substance (ODS), as identified by, and listed in
            the Montreal Protocol on Substances that Deplete the Ozone
            Layer. The CTC sector plan of the Government of India
            intends to reduce CTC production, and consumption to a level
            consistent with the obligations under the Montreal Protocol.
            This environmental assessment describes the CTC phase out
            schedule, and outlines the generic environmental and social
            aspects of the plan, including their implications in the
            chlorinated rubber sub-sector. Impacts likely to occur are
            further described,. Given there are no commercially
            available technologies in India to convert CTC to other
            non-ODS products, it is likely that exceeding quantities of
            CTC would have to be disposed of. Any technology options to
            eliminate unwanted quantities of CTC should not generate
            other environmental problems. Thus, the choice of technology
            to address this residual CTC production, should conform to
            the regulations, and policies of the Government. Moreover,
            any changes to chloromethane production facilities,
            resulting from the implementation of CTC phase out, should
            be subject to environmental permitting procedures. For metal
            cleaning operations, the use of chlorinated solvents -
            trichloroethylene and metallic chloride, aqueous
            technologies, as well as cleaning petroleum solvents, and
            alcohols -  are the most likely substitutes for CTC in
            solvent, and process agent applications. The final decision
            will have to be made on a case by case basis, by
            participating enterprises, and reviewed by the Ozone Cell
            through experts. Within the regulatory framework,
            enterprises are required to obtain approval from
            authorities, including the State Pollution Control Boards,
            and Factories Inspectorate. Verification of environmental
            aspects should entail assessment of processes, baseline
            environmental conditions, environmental management plans for
            dismantling and closure, manpower rehabilitation plans, and
            social monitoring plans with the involvement of communities.
            The verification is to be conducted by an independent audit,
            under the supervision of the Ozone Cell.'}

abstracts:
{'cdata!': 'This environmental management plan for
            the India ABIL Solid Waste Management Project anticipates
            negative impacts and proposes measures to mitigate them.
            Among the impacts described are: the deterioration of the
            ambient air quality due to stack emissions; and dust
            emissions due to waste transport by truck on unpaved roads;
            deterioration of ground and surface water quality due to
            leachate from the compost plant during the monsoon season
            and from indiscriminate dumping of waste and waste rejects
            during this season; odor nuisance from trucks carrying waste
            near the plant; water spills during transport; absence of a
            designated landfill site leading to indiscriminate dumping
            of inert/inorganic waste and rejects near the plant;
            accidental or unintended spills of waste residues or raw
            waste into forest areas; fire hazards to the plant and its
            surroundings during gas leakage from digestors/gas holders;
            and occupational health and safety hazards due to the
            movement of heavy vehicles, pests carrying pathogens,
            contaminated materials, and noxious gases. To mitigate
            impacts to air quality, complete the greenbelt project,
            upgrade the access road to the plant from Dubagga vegetable
            market, identify a sanitary landfill site for safe waste
            disposal. Monitor ground water quality. Segregate waste at
            the source. Provide a compost filtrate sump to collect the
            leachate from the compost; this leachate will be pumped to
            the pulpers for slurry preparation or sprayed over the
            compost to prevent charring of compost. Do regular
            maintenance checks to ensure proper functioning of the odor
            control system; cover trucks used for waste transport; use
            access routes to avoid residential neighborhoods; and speed
            truck inspections, weighing, and unloading to reduce truck
            waiting time. Formulate a contingency plan for fire safety,
            train staff, and conduct mock drills. Provide protective
            equipment such as masks and gloves for personnel working in
            the plant and do periodic health check ups for workers. Set
            up a public awareness program.'}

abstracts:
{'cdata!': 'This is an environmental assessment for
            the India Assam Agricultural Competitiveness Project (AACP),
            a follow-on project for the Assam Rural Infrastructure and
            Agriculture Services Project (ARIASP). The AACP aims to
            promote agricultural growth, promote development of small
            and marginal farmers, improve nutrition, and build the
            capacity of stakeholders. This report anticipates likely
            negative environmental impacts associated with the follow-on
            project and discusses measures to mitigate them. Measures to
            address and actions recommended include the following:
            Schedule construction to suit water availability and avoid
            water use conflicts. Get prior official clearance to fell
            trees and compensate for tree loss with replanting and
            landscaping. Relocate cultural properties to avoid damage.
            Avoid clearing vegetation beyond right-of-ways. Procure
            machinery that conforms to emission standards. Provide
            safety equipment for workers. To lessen pollution from
            materials extraction fro borrow and quarry areas, choose
            siting according to set criteria and avoid natural habitats.
            Dispose of or store grubbing waste and debris, and possibly
            reuse. Manage flooding by providing diversion channels
            and/or scheduling construction of culverts in dry months.
            Strip and store topsoil to mitigate loss. Control blasting
            as provided by law. Reduce emissions by covering trucks with
            tarpaulin during transport. To prevent water contamination
            from leaching, provide an impervious base to storage areas.
            Use dust suppressants like water to control particulates in
            air. Set aside areas for waste disposal. Schedule embankment
            construction in wet months, if possible. Use slope
            stabilization measures such as seeding, mulching, and
            bioengineering techniques. Construct temporary erosion
            control structures. Avoid disposal of liquid wastes into
            natural watercourses, and use silt fencing and vegetative
            barriers. Dispose of wastewater from labor camps into soak
            pits. Remove oil and clean up other chemical spills and
            wastes. Control sediment runoff. Restore campsite to
            original condition according to the rehabilitation plan.'}

            promote agricultural growth, promote development of small
            and marginal farmers, improve nutrition, and build the
            capacity of stakeholders. This report anticipates likely
            negative environmental impacts associated with the follow-on
            project and discusses measures to mitigate them. Measures to
            address and actions recommended include the following:
            Schedule construction to suit water availability and avoid
            water use conflicts. Get prior official clearance to fell
            trees and compensate for tree loss with replanting and
            landscaping. Relocate cultural properties to avoid damage.
            Avoid clearing vegetation beyond right-of-ways. Procure
            machinery that conforms to emission standards. Provide
            safety equipment for workers. To lessen pollution from
            materials extraction fro borrow and quarry areas, choose
            siting according to set criteria and avoid natural habitats.
            Dispose of or store grubbing waste and debris, and possibly
            reuse. Manage flooding by providing diversion channels
            and/or scheduling construction of culverts in dry months.
            Strip and store topsoil to mitigate loss. Control blasting
            as provided by law. Reduce emissions by covering trucks with
            tarpaulin during transport. To prevent water contamination
            from leaching, provide an impervious base to storage areas.
            Use dust suppressants like water to control particulates in
            air. Set aside areas for waste disposal. Schedule embankment
            construction in wet months, if possible. Use slope
            stabilization measures such as seeding, mulching, and
            bioengineering techniques. Construct temporary erosion
            control structures. Avoid disposal of liquid wastes into
            natural watercourses, and use silt fencing and vegetative
            barriers. Dispose of wastewater from labor camps into soak
            pits. Remove oil and clean up other chemical spills and
            wastes. Control sediment runoff. Restore campsite to

abstracts:
{'cdata!': 'Ratings for the Maharashtra Water Sector
            Improvement Project for India were as follows: outcomes were
            moderately satisfactory, risk to development outcome was
            moderate, Bank performance was moderately satisfactory, and
            Borrower performance was moderately satisfactory. Some
            lessons learned included: success of institutional reforms
            depends on level of government commitment. The focus should
            be on building client capacity for monitoring and evaluation
            (M and E) through training and investment in computerized
            systems instead of mostly relying on M and E consultants to
            carry out project M and E. The effectiveness of large
            infrastructure investments to rehabilitate and modernize
            irrigation systems for improved water use efficiency and
            productivity are considerably enhanced by the inclusion of a
            well-designed and well-implemented agricultural support
            services component. Information, education, and
            communication (IEC) activities were an important part of the
            project because of the significant and complex policy and
            institutional changes. A fundamental change in government
            procedures is needed to address the disconnect between: (a)
            increased water charges and collections that reflect full
            operation and maintenance (O and M) costs, and (b) low
            budget allocations for O and M. Consideration should be
            given to amending the Maharashtra Management of Irrigation
            Systems by Farmers (MMISF) Act to allow staggering of the
            election of representatives such that half the members are
            elected for a six year term every three years.'}

abstracts:
{'cdata!': "The Maharashtra Water Sector Improvement
            Project seeks to strengthen the State's capacity for
            multi-sectoral planning, development, and sustainable
            management of the water resources, and to improve irrigation
            service delivery, and productivity of irrigated agriculture.
            The project components provide support for institutional
            reforms, and capacity building in water resources management
            as well as irrigation service delivery, and complementary
            investments in improving and modernizing physical assets as
            described hereby. The first component - Water Sector
            Institutional Restructuring and Capacity Building - will
            support the establishment and operations of the Maharashtra
            Water Resources Regulatory Authority (MWRRA); restructure
            the existing Maharashtra Krishna Valley Development
            Corporation (MKVDC) into the Maharashtra Krishna Valley
            Water Resources Corporation (MKVWRC), as a river basin
            agency, and build it's capacity; restructure and
            strengthen the capacity of the Water Resources Department
            (WRD), and likewise, of the Water and Land Management
            Institute (WALMI). The component will finance the
            establishment of an integrated computerized information
            system (ICIS). The second component - improving Irrigation
            Service Delivery and Management - will support the
            participatory rehabilitation, and modernization of selected
            irrigation schemes within the Culturable Command Area (CCA).
            The component will further enhance the safety of selected
            dams, and will also focus on the formation and capacity
            building of Water User's Associations (WUAS) among
            selected irrigation schemes. Improved water management
            practices will be implemented, with the inclusion of various
            instruments in six selected irrigation schemes. Agriculture
            support services will be strengthened, in liaison with the
            implementation of the social and environmental management
            plan. Innovative Pilots will be supported through the third
            component, to prod the user-centered, aquifer level
            groundwater management, and other pilots for innovative
            irrigated agriculture. Finally, the fourth component will
            support the Project Preparation and Management Unit (PPMIJ)
            at the state level, and, support monitoring and evaluation,
            as well as an information, education, and communication
            campaign to create awareness on project initiatives."}

display_title: India - Maharashtra Water Sector             Improvement Project : resettlement plan
abstracts:
{'cdata!': "The Maharashtra Water Sector Improvement
            Project seeks to strengthen the state's capacity for
            multi-sectoral planning, developments, and sustainable
            management of water resources, and, to improve irrigation
            service delivery, to increase productivity of irrigated
            agriculture. It is nonetheless envisaged that resettlement
            will occur, and to this end, this resettlement and
            entitlement framework sets the rationale, and guidelines for
            the resettlement process. Loss of land will be compensated
            in cash, free of cost and registration fees. Provided there
            is a major displacement, provisions of Schedule (Part IV) as
            per Act 2001 will be applied, plus registration charges.
            Non-title holders will provided with new housing at selected
            sites free of cost and registration charges, with same
            provisions as above for major displacement. Affected
            families due to agricultural land losses, will have the
            option between cash compensation plus alternate land at
            occupancy fixed price; or, cash compensation plus
            rehabilitation assistance equal to a minimum agricultural
            wages of a) 750 days for those losing entire land, b) 500
            days for those losing part of land, but becoming marginal
            farmers, and, c) 375 days for those losing part of land and
            becoming small farmers; or, cash compensation plus option of
            equivalent amount for regular income. Tenants will be
            reimbursed for unexpired lease. Although not eligible for
            compensation, encroachers however, particularly the
            vulnerable, will be eligible for support for regular income.
            Loss of housing and physical structures will be compensated
            in cash plus permission to take salvaged materials, plus
            allotment of house site, and assistance for construction,
            and support during transition. Business losses will be
            compensated in cash for the structure, pus a fixed amount
            for construction of new business structure and support
            during transition. Squatters will be reimbursed for
            unexpired lease. Crop and fruit bearing tree losses will be
            compensated at market values."}

display_title: India - Maharashtra Water Sector             Improvement Project : indigenous peoples plan
abstracts:
{'cdata!': "The objectives Maharashtra Water Sector
            Improvement Project for India are: (i) to strengthen the
            state's capacity for multisectoral planning,
            development, and sustainable management of the water
            resources, and (ii) to improve irrigation service delivery
            on a sustainable basis to increase productivity of irrigated
            agriculture and contribute to rural poverty reduction. In
            Maharashtra, nearly one-tenth of the state's population
            is constituted by scheduled tribes. Tribal is largely
            concentrated in the western hilly Districts of Dhule,
            Nandurbar, Jalgaon, Nashik and Thane (Shyadri Region) and
            the eastern forests Districts of Chandrapur, Gadchiroli,
            Bhandara, Gondia, Nagpur, Amravati and Yavatmal (Gondwana
            Region). Thus twelve of the 35 districts in the state have
            been identified as scheduled areas under the Fifth Schedule
            of the Constitution of India, that is, areas that have
            significant proportion of population as tribals. The Project
            will cover 6 of the 12 tribal districts. These districts are
            Ahemdnagar, Thane, Nanded, Jalgaon, Amaravati, and Gadchiroli."}

display_title: India - Maharashtra Water Sector             Improvement Project : integrated social and environmental             assessment study : Environmental assessment - Main report
abstracts:
{'cdata!': 'This is a social and environmental
            assessment for the Maharashtra Water Sector Improvement
            Project. Most of the activities in the implementation phase
            related to asset improvement will lead to short-term
            reversible impacts. For situations where moderate, long-term
            and negative impacts are anticipated, a two-tiered
            mitigation strategy is proposed, consisting of
            activity-specific recommendations and a programmatic
            approach, to address the long-term and second order social
            and environmental impacts and ensure both effectiveness and
            sustainability of the project. Expected impacts comprise
            land encroachment, disturbance of ecosystem and
            biodiversity, ecological impacts due to tree and shrub
            cutting, disruption of utilities, more traffic, damage to
            existing structures due to site clearance, earthwork
            excavation, and materials storage; canal, well, and aquifer
            obstruction caused by silt, clay, sand, and soil; noise;
            dust; air pollution from vehicle exhaust; topsoil removal;
            and damage to cultural relics.   Minimize land acquisition
            and pay compensation; avoid eco-sensitive areas; replant
            trees; avoid using farmland, forest belts, and arable land
            for borrow sites; safeguard utilities and get approvals in
            advance; regulate traffic and plan alternate routes; avoid
            dumping on private land; restore sites, locate site after
            public consultation, and keep site clean; encourage
            participation of vulnerable groups; avoid wetlands and
            riparian areas; locate burrow pits and quarries so as to
            minimize land impacts; drain pits to provide safe access,
            stop water ponds, and minimize the spread of water-borne
            diseases; ensure unobstructed drains; dispose of surplus
            excavated earth; provide for environmental emergencies; safe
            collection and disposal of solid waste; restrict operations
            near sensitive areas during day; avoid construction
            activities at night; provide protective gear against noise;
            maintain vehicles to meet emissions standards and noise
            control; install sound barriers; warn before blasting; damp
            down earthworks and haul roads; replace topsoil; and
            preserve cultural relics.'}

display_title: India - Maharashtra Water Sector             Improvement Project : Environmental assessment executive summary
abstracts:
{'cdata!': "The Maharashtra Water Sector Improvement
            Project seeks to strengthen the state's capacity for
            multi-sectoral planning, developments, and sustainable
            management of the water resources, and, to improve
            irrigation service delivery, to increase productivity of
            irrigated agriculture. To this end, this executive summary
            provides a brief outlook on relevant social, environmental,
            and sectoral policies, and regulatory framework that govern
            the water sector. It analyzes existing data regarding
            participatory irrigation management, the agriculture
            situation, and environmental issues associated with
            irrigation projects. The Social and Environmental Management
            Framework (SEMF) sets the road map to be followed during
            project implementation, based on a step-by-step methodology
            of activities, to be undertaken in parallel to institutional
            and engineering project intervention measures. The SEMF
            contains formats and checklists to ensure relevant
            environmental issues are addressed in each subproject, as
            well as strategies - action plans and recommendations - for
            key issues such as resettlement, and tribal development. For
            situations where moderate, long-term and negative impacts
            are anticipated, the SEMF proposes a two-tiered mitigation
            strategy: 1) Mitigation at activity level - Specific
            recommendations are given on how the activity should be
            performed with modifications/best practices, outlining
            allocation of responsibilities, and needed monitoring
            measures; and, 2) Mitigation at programmatic level -
            Recommendations are given on developing/strengthening
            supportive programs such as tribal development, sustainable
            agriculture, gender participation, etc. The SEMF prescribes
            specific measures for each stage of the sub-project cycle:
            Preparation - planning and design - Implementation, and,
            operation stages - i.e., to monitor and assess the long-term
            impacts of project interventions. Following consultations
            with stakeholders, sensitization/awareness is recommended,
            particularly as it concerns subprojects and the relevant
            sample reconnaissance surveys in those selected
            sub-projects. Strategic action plans triggered dam safety
            plans; a sustainable agriculture strategy covering
            irrigation planning management, flood and drainage
            management plans; soil conservation planning; groundwater
            restoration plans; pollution management planning; silt
            disposal and utilization; and as well, resettlement, and
            tribal development plans. Environmental management training
            should be provided, to be focused in line with proposed
            physical activities of the subprojects. Contract documents
            shall include precautionary clauses regarding technical
            specifications, and contractors' responsibilities in
            line with environmental regulations. Monitoring and
            evaluation of environmental parameters, as identified
            herein, shall ensure compliance."}

            have recently gained centre stage in explaining variations
            in competitiveness, growth and prosperity across countries
            or regions.  The investment climate comprises  institutional
            and policy variables that have a crucial bearing on business
            performance, but over which firms have no control
            individually.  Key determinants of the investment climate
            include the functioning of product and factor markets;
            sources of non-pecuniary intra- and inter-industry
            externalities (i.e., spillovers)  the quality of public
            goods (such as law and order, government regulation) and
            their effects on the cost of borrowing, on price stability,
            or on exchange rates via fiscal and monetary policies; and
            some physical and social infrastructure.  The report
            asseses India's investment climate from the perspective
            of industrial growth and focuses on investment climate
            variations within India, analyzing the implications these
            variations have on industrial performance, as well as,
            subnational disparities in productivity and growth."}

            Hydrology Project for India were as follows: outcomes were
            moderately satisfactory, risk to development outcome was
            negligible to low, Bank performance was moderately
            satisfactory, and Borrower performance was moderately
            satisfactory. Some lessons learned included: for technically
            innovative and institutionally complex projects such as the
            establishment of hydrological information system (HIS)
            across India, a long-term programmatic and demand driven
            approach is required, allowing each implementing agency (IA)
            to progress at its own pace and evolving needs. Central
            agencies need to take a spearheading role regarding HIS data
            exchange and dissemination, in order to accelerate the
            present paradigm shift towards river basin planning and
            integrated water resources management (IWRM) in India.
            Integration of state surface water (SW) and ground water
            (GW) departments and (particularly) state data centers
            facilitates and promotes the integration of SW and GW data
            analyses, enables the adoption of an IWRM approach at state
            level, and improves joint project management and
            implementation. Web-based data processing and storage
            systems facilitate easy accessibility across the country,
            central annual maintenance contract (AMC) and help desk
            functions, and reduce potential future licensing issues.

            economic and financial analysis - need to implement

abstracts:
{'cdata!': 'The Tamil Nadu Urban Infrastructure
            Financial Services Limited (TNUIFSL) has been set up to
            manage a Trust fund  -Tamil Nadu Urban Development Fund
            (TNUDF). The TNUDF has been established to manage urban
            infrastructure projects under the Third Tamil Nadu
            Development Project. This Environmental and Resettlement
            Framework document (ERF) outlines the policies, assessments
            and procedures that will enable TNUIFSL to ensure that a
            project that it funds is developed in accordance with the
            ERF and is adequately protected from environmental and
            social risks. The ERF also aims to sensitize borrowers to
            the assessment and management of environmental and social
            issues arising in urban infrastructure projects.
            Environmental and social impacts mitigation measures include
            : address legitimate concerns of relevant stakeholders,
            especially project affected persons (PAP); avoid or minimize
            resettlement and rehabilitation of PAPs due to land
            acquisition; ensure appropriate resettlement and
            rehabilitation to provide sustainable livelihood options;
            protect marginalized and vulnerable groups, including the
            economically and socially disadvantaged; develop a plan to
            minimize health and safety hazards; monitor all subprojects
            to ensure conformity environmental and social standards;
            sprinkling of water and removal of construction debris from
            sites as soon as possible; use of less noise generating
            machinery, provide personal protective equipment, ear muffs,
            etc., during construction, and avoid  nocturnal construction
            activities; ensure that private contractor provides
            appropriate housing, water supply, and sanitation facilities
            to construction laborers; provide adequate and safe sludge
            disposal facilities to avoid land and surface water
            contamination; and finally, ensure safe operation and
            maintenance practices are followed and emergency plans are
            in place.'}

abstracts:
{'cdata!': "This resettlement action plan (RAP) in
            compliance with the Third Tamil Nadu Urban Development
            Project for India objectives, seeks to avoid (as possible)
            land acquisition in the forest areas, private lands or
            damage to structures; ensure that the alignment doesn't
            require acquisition of private agriculture lands or
            properties; avoid acquisition of forest or provide lands;
            ensure that, no dense habitations or sensitive features such
            as schools, religious places or institutions are located in
            the vicinity or project area; ensure the site is not located
            in highly populated or congested areas; avoid a site that
            requires relocation of population (pucca or kutcha houses or
            slums/squatters or encroaches); ensure that the laying and
            operation of alignment does not affect agricultural lands,
            farming operations, crops and their yield. Compensation will
            be in the form of land for land replacement to the extent
            lost, subject to a maximum of 1 ha of wet land, or 2 ha of
            dry land; the project affected person (PAP) will have the
            option of either retaining the assigned plot or taking cash
            compensation. The project will provide one time financial
            assistance equivalent to 750 days minimum agricultural
            wages. Transitional assistance equivalent to six month
            minimum wages will be provided, and, the right to salvage
            material will be allowed as possible. Alternate resettlement
            sites shall be provided with a dwelling unit as per
            Government norms. Squatters will be provided a one time
            shifting allowance of Rs.5000/ and the right to salvage
            material, while encroachers will be compensated with a six
            month rental allowance to re-establish residence. Regarding
            non-perennial crops, 4 months notice will be given for
            harvesting, and, if land is acquired before harvesting, a
            grant equivalent to market value of crops lost, plus the
            cost of replacement of seeds for the next season's
            planting of perennial crops and trees; the grant paid is
            calculated at annual produce value of 15 years. Moving
            expenses will be provided, and grievance mechanisms will be
            in place should conflict occur."}

India - Country assistance strategy
abstracts:
{'cdata!': "This Country Assistance Strategy (CAS)
            for the period FY05-08 seeks to build a strong partnership
            with the Government of India, and, its overarching challenge
            will be how to maximize, and leverage Bank resources, to
            significantly scale up impacts, improve the quality of life
            of the poorest citizens, and help India achieve the
            Millennium Development Goals (MDGs). Three strategic
            principles will underpin the Bank's work: 1) focusing
            on outcomes; 2) applying selectivity; and, 3) expanding the
            Bank's role as a politically, realistic knowledge
            provider, and generator. This expansion will primarily be in
            a) infrastructure - transport, power, water supply and
            sanitation, irrigation, and urban development; b) human
            development - education, health, social protection; and, c)
            rural livelihoods, emphasizing on community-driven
            approaches. During the period, important shifts are
            envisioned in the use of new approaches, i.e., cofinancing,
            and sector-wide approaches, where the Bank will seek
            engagement, and partnerships for this assistance. While the
            strategy will retain a reform, and performance-based
            approach to the states, it will change in the ways intended
            to engage with the largest, and poorest states, through
            policy dialogues on cross-cutting reforms - fiscal
            management, governance, service delivery, power sector, and
            investment climate. The CAS calls for enhanced focus on
            major analytical work, and a substantially higher level of
            International Development Association (IDA) resources, while
            the Bank's lending would fall within a range limited by
            an upper bound, which will require strong reform
            performance, and a strengthened pace of project preparation."}

display_title: India - Karnataka Urban Water             Sector Improvement Project
abstracts:
{'cdata!': "The long-term vision for the urban water
            sector in the State of Karnataka, is to turn its performance
            into high quality, sustainable services in all urban local
            bodies; the strategy to achieve this vision is to implement
            a phased program towards full service coverage, and quality
            service provision in a sustainable manner. The Karnataka
            Urban Water sector Improvement Project components will: a)
            assist the State Government in finalizing its policy reform
            agenda, and carry out initial implementation steps of staged
            sector reforms; and, to prepare business model, and private
            sector participation processes for service provision in

            provision, and attain continuous service in selected
            demonstration zones; generate credibility in the overall
            program and learn lessons on the challenges faced in the
            demonstration zones for scaling up continuous service
            provision; and, simultaneously improve the efficiency of
            bulk supply operations, and distribution networks, attaining
            initial improvements in water service provision to all State
            residents. The third component will finance the
            project's incremental operational costs, and studies
            related to project management and implementation, including
            incremental, short term consultants for the Karnataka Urban
            Infrastructure Development and Finance Corporation (KUIDFC);
            the preparation and establishment of a monitoring and
            evaluation system; the costs related to the financial
            management systems within KUIDFC; staff training within
            KUIDFC Project Management Unit; and, the incremental
            operating cost at KUIDFC, including supervision costs."}

abstracts:
{'cdata!': "The Karnataka Urban Water and Sanitation
            Sector Improvement Project entails infrastructure water

            benefits to end users. However, it is also foreseen that
            land acquisition, and resettlement will occur as a result of

            operational directive on involuntary resettlement. Affected
            people should include as well vulnerable groups, such as
            women headed families, and groups below the poverty line,
            who will be eligible for a one time additional income

            resettlement will be negotiated, to be acceptable by
            affected people. Likewise, other assets lost due to land

            losses, and the usage of land that may be imposed, will be
            compensated at 25 percent of the market value of affected

            Monitoring will be in place to ensure the appropriate

display_title: India - Karnataka Water Supply             and Sanitation Sector Improvement Project : environmental assessment
abstracts:
{'cdata!': 'The sectoral reform nature of the
            Karnataka Urban Water and Sanitation Sector Improvement
            Project, will take place gradually, and incrementally,
            launched through small-scale demonstration projects in three
            urban places - Gulbarga, Belgaum, and Hubli-Dharwad.
            However, the proposed investments to the existing system for
            continuous water supply will potentially alter local water
            supply distribution, causing leakages, and flooding. This
            environmental assessment looks at potential environmental
            adversity resulting from the implementation of the project,
            and provides the following mitigation measures: adequate
            flushing, and bypass arrangements should be planned for the
            city, to avoid water wastes, flooding, and water
            contamination; surfaces on construction sites should be
            water sprayed regularly to minimize dust emissions, ensuring
            as well adequate removal of construction debris; alternative
            water supply provisions should be in place, i.e., tanker
            supply, and, appropriate bypass, and leak control
            arrangements ensured; traffic diversion plans, and traffic
            safety measures should be implemented during construction;
            safety precautions should be readily available to workers,
            such as helmets, safety shoes, gloves, etc.; temporary
            drainage arrangements, possibly natural drainage, should be
            established to prevent surface water runoff, or water
            pollution; waste disposal should be transported to selected
            disposal sites; extensive communication campaigns should be
            conducted to increase awareness among local communities;
            chemicals, and hazardous material (e.g., chlorine cylinders)
            should be handled with care, and properly stored; detailed
            engineering designs shall ensure the safe passage of storm
            waters into existing channels during the operation phase;
            and, earth works, and construction activities shall be
            minimized by refilling, and replacing excavated topsoil into
            the same field, and soil barriers will be installed to avoid
            spillage, particularly on agricultural lands.'}

            contribution to reduction of public sector borrowing in

India - Scaling-up access to             finance for India's rural poor
abstracts:
{'cdata!': 'Since the early national plans,
            successive governments in independent India have emphasized
            the link between improving access to finance, and reducing
            poverty - a stance that has had influence globally. The need
            to improve financial access for India's poor, the
            overwhelming majority of whom are concentrated in rural
            areas, motivated the nationalization of commercial banks in
            the late 1960s, and an aggressive drive through the 1970s
            and 1980s, to expand rural banking, coupled with policies
            mandating banks to provide subsidized credit to rural
            households. The 1990s saw the partial deregulation of
            interest rates, a gradual reduction in the Government's
            stake in commercial banks, and increased competition in the
            banking sector. Access to finance for the rural poor has
            improved somewhat over the past decades, with the public
            sector commercial banks being the dominant players in the
            formal rural finance market. Yet, the vast majority of
            India's rural poor, still do not have access t o formal
            finance. The report examines the reasons, and factors
            affecting both banks, and their clients. First is the
            problem of uncertainty - about the repayment capacity of
            poor rural borrowers, and their irregular/volatile income
            streams and expenditure patterns - which, in the absence of
            credit information, drive up default risk. Second, the
            transactions costs of rural lending in India are high,
            mainly due to small loan sizes, high frequency of
            transactions, large geographical spread, and heterogeneity
            of borrowers, and widespread illiteracy. Third, the
            Government policies have made things worse from the
            banks' perspective, creating a "financial
            climate" not conducive to lending in general, and rural
            banking in particular. New approaches and products to
            improve rural access to finance in India are reviewed,
            namely, the 'Self-help Groups (SHGs) Bank Linkage'
            model, the growth of which - from just 500 SHGs linked to
            banks in the early 1990s, to over 700,000 in 2003 - has been
            truly remarkable; specialized microfinance institutions;
            and, partnerships between private Banks,, micro-financiers,
            and service providers, including the Kisan Credit Card.
            Furthermore, a potential means of reducing default risk in
            rural finance, that has recently caught the attention of the
            Government, is the establishment of a "warehouse
            receipts system' to cover the agricultural risk
            management of products for farmers. The policy agenda to
            improve access to finance by the rural poor looks at
            introducing flexible products; the need for composite
            financial services; simplified procedures to access finance;
            and, improved staffing policies and doorstep banking,
            including an enabling policy, legal and regulatory
            environment for micro-finance.While the importance of
            microfinance in consumption-easing should not be
            underestimated, its success in budding up poor peoples'
            assets, over the medium term, would much depend on efforts
            directed at providing assistance in skills development,
            technology and marketing - all of which are critical to
            ensuring that investments made by poor households, reap
            returns and contribute to a sustained increase in incomes
            and improvements in rural livelihoods.'}

display_title: Microfinance in India - banyan             Tree and bonsai : a review paper for the World Bank
abstracts:
{'cdata!': "This paper is about microfinance, not
            only about microfinance institutions (MFIs). It deals with
            the whole range of microfinance providers from the village
            mahajan to self-help groups (SHGs) to cooperatives, banks
            and insurance companies.   The paper is also not just about
            micro-credit but microfinance covering savings, insurance,
            credit, and money transfers.  Finally, the paper is about
            the future but it also dwells on the past and the present,
            since there are lessons to be learnt from experience.  The
            central thesis of this paper is that since the onset of
            reforms, the mainstream financial sector has turned its back
            to the needs of India's small farmers and informal
            sector producers.   In the meanwhile, the growth of
            micro-credit, mainly through SHGs, is distracting attention
            from the big picture of the systematic financial exclusion
            of the majority. Village moneylenders in India are as old as
            villages, agricultural credit cooperatives are about a
            hundred years old, commercial banks' involvement in
            agricultural and small loans nearly 50 years old, the
            regional rural bank network over 25 years old, and the first
            'new generation' microfinance efforts about 10
            years old.  Thus microfinance in India is still in its
            infancy, though its growth rate is impressive, and
            particularly the SHG-bank linkage program appears to have
            the potential of becoming a big banyan  tree. However, the
            microfinance sector in context of the unmet demand, the
            image that comes to mind is that of a bonsai."}

abstracts:
{'cdata!': 'Ratings for the Integrated Watershed
            Development Project for India were as follows: outcomes were
            moderately unsatisfactory risk to development outcome was
            significant, Bank performance was moderately satisfactory,

            Ratings for the Karnataka Watershed Development Project for
            India were as follows: outcomes were satisfactory risk to
            development outcome was moderate, Bank performance was
            moderately satisfactory, and borrower performance was
            satisfactory. Ratings for the Andhra Pradesh Community
            Forestry Management Project for India were as follows:
            outcomes were moderately satisfactory, risk to development
            outcome was significant, Bank performance was moderately
            satisfactory, and borrower performance was satisfactory.
            Some lessons learned includes: this report assesses a mix of
            Bank-supported activities intended to further watershed
            development and improve forest management. A handy
            portmanteau definition of watershed development is as
            follows: a watershed may be defined as a geographic area
            that drains to a common point. Integrated watershed
            development is generally understood as an approach that
            combines soil and water conservation with social and
            institutional development, in addition to pursuing a broad
            range of activities that meet the felt needs of communities
            across many sectors, such as rural access, water supply, and
            income-generating activities.  Assessing watershed
            development and forest interventions side-by-side is no idle
            juxtaposition. Obviously, all forests fall within watersheds
            so there is some merit to having a natural resources
            management strategy that includes both.  In designing
            watershed and forest interventions there is a common theme.
            Both types of project are beset by problems of property
            rights that have been incompletely specified or questionably
            assigned or are simply missing. This report assesses two
            watershed development projects and one forestry project. The
            objectives of the watershed development projects in the
            Shivalik Hills and in Karnataka were similar: both sought to
            improve the productive potential of selected watersheds and
            to build the institutions needed for improved management of
            the natural resource base, including community organizations.'}

abstracts:
{'cdata!': "This report provides an assessment of
            accounting and auditing practices in India, within the
            broader context of institutional capacity available for
            ensuring high-quality financial reporting. India's
            accounting profession was among the earliest to develop
            historically, when the Indian Companies Act was enacted in
            the mid-l800s, giving the accounting profession its start.
            Since then, considerable efforts have been made to align
            India's accounting and auditing standards and
            practices, with the internationally accepted standards and
            codes. In order to further improve the quality of corporate
            financial reporting in India, there is a need to improve the
            institutional framework, and take steps for enhancing
            compliance with the applicable standards and rules. Enhanced
            by significant inputs from stakeholders, this report
            provides some principles-based policy recommendations aimed
            at strengthening the corporate financial reporting regime in
            India. These recommendations specifically focus on
            strengthening the monitoring and enforcement arrangements.
            Moreover, suggestions have been made on some important
            elements for an independent oversight body for the auditing
            profession, from a public interest perspective. The
            objectives of the recommendations are to build on the
            existing system, and promote a gradual process of improvement."}

India - Economic Growth and             Poverty Alleviation in Tamil Nadu: notes on selected policy issues
abstracts:
{'cdata!': 'Tamil Nadu faces the longer-term
            challenge of reform for accelerating economic growth and
            reducing poverty. Repeated droughts and growing waters
            shortages have heightened the importance of structural
            transformation. Such transformation will reduce the
            vulnerability of the economy to periodic drought, and free
            up scarce water resources to higher value-addition
            activities in the industrial and service sectors. The faster
            growth of these two sectors would help absorb agriculture
            surplus labor and reduce currently high unemployment rate of
            the state. Reform priorities for the structural
            transformation to accelerate economic growth and reducing
            poverty are: Fiscal stabilization, correcting aggregate
            imbalances, and improving the composition of expenditure is
            critical for creating the fiscal space for priority spending
            in infrastructure and social sectors. Fiscal reform must be
            accompanied by strengthened public expenditure management
            and public administration to improve the effectiveness of
            public spending and service delivery. Fiscal adjustment
            alone without a complementary focus on the investment
            climate and economic growth is insufficient. Faster economic

Why don't poor countries do             R&D ?
abstracts:
{'cdata!': "Using a global panel on research and
            development (R&D) expenditures, this paper documents
            that on average poor countries do far less R&D than rich
            as a share of GDP. This is arguably counter intuitive since
            the gains from doing the R&D required for technological
            catch up are thought to be very high and Griffith et al
            (2004) have documented that in the OECD returns increase
            dramatically with distance from the frontier. Exploiting
            recent advances in instrumental variables in a varying
            coefficient context we find that the rates of return follow
            an inverted U: they rise with distance to the frontier and
            then fall thereafter, potentially turning negative for the
            poorest countries. The findings are consistent with the
            importance of factors complementary to R&D, such as
            education, the quality of scientific infrastructure and the
            overall functioning of the national innovation system, and
            the quality of the private sector, which become increasingly
            weak with distance from the frontier and the absence of
            which can offset the catch up effect. China's and
            India's explosive growth in R&D investment
            trajectories in spite of expected low returns may be
            justified by their importing the complementary factors in
            the form of multinational corporations who do most of the
            patentable research."}

abstracts:
{'cdata!': "The Government of India (GOI) and the
            Government of Tamil Nadu (GOTN) strategic priorities are
            reflected in this project, as per the Tenth Plan and Human
            Resource Development Report. GOTN's strategy focuses on
            more effective targeting of the poor, building and
            strengthening local grass-roots organizations and Panchayat
            level institutions, and building local level partnerships,
            increasing livelihood opportunities and access to economic
            activities, while mainstreaming gender into development
            programs. Project activities entail construction works,
            creation of micro enterprises, rural infrastructure,
            including roads and bridges, and agriculture based micro
            processing industries, to name a few. This environmental
            assessment addresses adverse environmental impacts
            associated with project investments, in line with
            India's laws and regulations concerning the
            environment, and the Bank's operational directive on
            the subject. Overall, mitigation measures stipulate the
            following. To avoid or minimize air pollution: construction
            materials should be stored, or covered to prevent dust
            emissions; water spraying should be conducted regularly; an
            equipment suppression system should be established to
            contain air particles; wind breaking walls shall be
            constructed, and metallic pathways installed around the
            project area; and, vegetative propagation ensured along the
            construction perimeter. Measures to protect, and conserve
            water include: protection of surface water drains to prevent
            water pollution; drainage systems should be inspected
            regularly to avoid contaminated discharges; water runoffs
            from refueling areas should be isolated from the regular
            drainage, to be re-directed, and drained into an oil
            separator; similarly, chemicals, and lubricants should be
            adequately stored. Disposal of solid wastes call for:
            establishment of a leachate collection and treatment system;
            appropriately separate wastes, either to be stored, or
            disposed at selected sites; and, empty containers,
            particularly if containing harmful residues, should be
            stored, and disposed of in compliance with standard regulations."}
