display_title: India - Fiscal Decentralization             to Rural Governments
abstracts:
{'cdata!': 'The objective of this study is to review
            panchayat finances, identify issues and make recommendations
            to improve the fiscal decentralization system. Using
            Kamataka and Kerala as case studies, this report describes
            the context for rural decentralization in India, summarizes
            the current fiscal situation of district, block and village
            panchayats, identifies the main problems arising from the
            current practice, and outlines a set of reform options that
            might better satisfy the objectives of the central and state
            governments. Kamataka and Kerala were examined because these
            two states are generally thought to be more advanced than
            others in implementing rural fiscal decentralization and are
            therefore relevant for drawing lessons for the rest of
            India. There is a hierarchical arrangement of
            center-state-local governance. The 73rd Amendment to the
            Constitution made India one of the most politically
            decentralized countries in the developing world. By the
            Constitution and in practice, local government has an urban
            and a rural stream. Rural local governments are divided into
            three levels: district (zilla), block (taluk), and village
            (gram) panchayats. The design and implementation of the
            decentralization program are a state government
            responsibility. However implementation of key aspects of the
            program is lagging. Districts and blocks have no taxing
            powers and little expenditure autonomy. Both in Karnataka
            and Kerala, they more or less function as spending agents of
            higher-level governments. Gram panchayats are closest to the
            people, have some independent taxing power, and some
            discretion in expenditure decisions. Hence they are the
            primary subjects of this study.'}

abstracts:
{'cdata!': "The Gujarat Emergency Earthquake
            Reconstruction Program Project's main objectives are:
            promoting sustainable recovery to the earthquake affected
            areas; and laying the foundation for sustainable disaster
            management capacity in Gujarat. There are four project
            components. The first finances the implementation of
            owner-driven housing recovery plans initiated under the
            ongoing immediate phase (Phase 1) for the partially damaged
            and fully collapsed houses in the affected rural and urban
            areas. The second component funds for repairing,
            strengthening, rehabilitating, reconstructing, and upgrading
            damaged public buildings, roads and bridges, and dams and
            irrigation infrastructure in the earthquake-affected areas;
            2) retrofitting undamaged government administration
            buildings and critically important public buildings and
            preparing detailed engineering documents for retrofitting
            key bridges; and 3) constructing buildings and control rooms
            needed to foster State emergency management as well as
            setting up the Gujarat Institute of Disaster Management
            (GIDM) and the Institute for Seismic Research. The third
            component ensures the participation of earthquake-affected
            communities establishing village-level subcenters to build
            capacity for earthquake-resistant construction,
            strengthening local government mechanisms, gender
            sensitization, and community-based disaster preparedness
            programs. The fourth component finances the establishment of
            a professional emergency management program."}

display_title: India - Gujarat Emergency             Earthquake Reconstruction Project : environmental assessment
abstracts:
{'cdata!': 'This environmental assessment for the
            Gujarat Emergency Earthquake Reconstruction Project
            describes negative environmental impacts and measures to be
            taken to mitigate them. An awareness campaign will be
            conducted so that excavated materials at each site will be
            managed properly, and storage/piling is done away from water
            bodies and drainage channels. Villages will be involved in
            the planning and site selection. No forestland, ecological
            protected areas, national parks, wildlife sanctuaries, or
            known habitats of flora/fauna will be acquired for public
            use, nor will environmental resources be overused as
            building materials. Pollution from and in the construction
            camps, loss of roadside vegetation, change in water
            availability, pollution of riverbeds (where bridges are
            built), management of borrow areas/quarries, and pollution
            from hot-mix and batching plants will be governed and/or
            alleviated using standard guidelines for
            mitigation/management of construction-related impacts in
            contractual provisions. All construction codes for buildings
            safety and worker safety will be strictly implemented.
            During construction activities, standard construction codes
            for minimizing environmental concerns will be used to offset
            increase of the catchment/submergence area due to increased
            dam height, and spillover and dust from haulage, storage,
            and handling of earth. The codes include provisions for
            efficient storage, haulage, handling of earthwork, dust
            suppression, and erosion control.'}

display_title: India - Power sector reform and             the poor
abstracts:
{'cdata!': 'Of all developing countries India has
            the largest number of poor, as measured by income, health,
            opportunities and access to basic needs. The national and
            state governments have carried out a number of initiatives
            affecting the poor. Of those initiatives, this report
            focuses on power sector reform efforts, carried out by some
            Indian states in the mid-1990s. It also aims to answer these
            questions: What are the main challenges that power reform
            faces in reducing poverty in India? What are the main
            obstacles and main opportunities? Are the large subsidies to
            the power sector reaching the poor? How are the poor
            affected by the present conditions of power supply and what
            changes will benefit them most?. In seeking answers to these
            questions, the report draws on relevant data and studies in
            India, as well as evidence from the literature and
            international experience with power sector reform. In view
            of an ongoing World Bank study on rural electrification that
            analyzes access issues, and the fact that tariff rebalancing
            is a major issue, this report focuses on the impact of
            electricity prices, quality of power supply, access issues,
            and subsidies to the poor.'}

abstracts:
{'cdata!': "The Allahabad Bypass Project (ABP) aims
            to (i) reduce transport constraints on national economic
            activity, and (ii) improve institutional capabilities to
            manage road programs, assets, and services on a more
            commercial basis. It is the third Bank loan to support the
            Government of  India's (GOI) National Highway
            Development Program (NHDP), which aims to upgrade 13,000 km
            of  core national highways network by 2007. The first two
            loans, namely the Third National Highway Project (TNHP)
            (rep. no. 20219)and Grand Trunk Road Improvement Project
            (GTRIP) (rep. no. 22169), were approved in June 2000 and
            June 2001, respectively. All three projects finance the
            upgrading of National Highway 2 between Delhi and Kolkata
            and support institutional strengthening actions.  There are
            three project components.   Component 1, bypass
            construction, funds the construction of  the 84.7 km bypass,
            which is located at the northern outskirts of  Allahabad
            City. The bypass will be an access controlled highway, with
            a 1 km bridge over the Ganga River. Toll plazas and rest
            areas will also be provided. Component 2 funds corridor
            management. Specifically, the component will fund the

abstracts:
{'cdata!': "The Allahabad Bypass Project includes
            alignments passing entirely through plain agricultural
            fields, and through rural settings within a number of
            villages, an influence area where agriculture is the
            mainstay of local populations, mostly farmers belonging to
            small, and marginal groups, and includes a variety of crops
            grown in the region. This Resettlement Action Plan (RAP)
            assesses the negative social impacts of the project, and
            suggests socioeconomic rehabilitation measures, in order to
            improve, or at least restore, the living conditions of
            project affected people (PAP). Based on socioeconomic, and
            census surveys, and in consultation with stakeholders, the
            RAP determines the following measures to minimize adverse
            social impacts resulting from project implementation. The
            project will seek to redesign intersections as possible, to
            avoid unnecessary loss of land, and structures, while
            service roads will be constructed to provide easy access,
            but under strict enforcement of parking, and traffic safety
            measures to discipline the traffic flow. Compensation will
            be provided at replacement values for loss of land, and
            physical structures, which includes the provision of
            drainage facilities; loss of crops, trees, and orchards,
            will be compensated based on estimated market values, while
            irrigation units will be replaced by the project; a
            double-story shopping complex should be built on nearby
            Government land, to accommodate demolished shops and
            businesses, and alternative income restoration will be
            considered; training will be provided to promote self
            employment opportunities, in line with the Government's
            poverty alleviation schemes; vulnerable groups will be given
            special consideration for their resettlement/rehabilitation
            needs, on priority bases; and, public awareness campaigns,
            monitoring, and grievance mechanisms will be established to

India - Allahabad Bypass Project             : environmental assessment executive summary
abstracts:
{'cdata!': 'This environmental assessment for the
            Allahabad Bypass Project details expected negative
            environmental impacts and their mitigations. Planting
            vegetation along the median and lanscaping along the
            corridor will help restore green cover. In selecting borrow
            areas, productive agricultural areas have been avoided as
            far as possible. Topsoilw ill be stripped and stored in
            stockpiles to be used to cover all disturbed areas including
            borrow areas, for top dressing of the road embankments and
            fill slopes; for filling up of tree pits in the median; and
            in the agricultural fields of farmers, acquired temporarily.
            To prevent soil erosion, turf high embankments with jute
            mesh, among other materials; and line with stone pitching
            and filter blankets to control erosion for channel changes
            of steams and canals. The size and shape of borrow pits will
            be controlled in cultivable land, non-cultivable land, and
            by the riverside; precautionary measures like the covering
            of vehicles will avoid spillage during transport of borrow
            materials as well as quarry materials. Vehicles and
            equipment will be maintained and refueled so as to avoid
            oil/diesel spillage; fuel storage and refueling sites will
            be located away from drainage channels, major rivers, canals
            and other water bodies; oil intereceptors will be used; and
            spills and petroleum products will be disposed of according
            to pre-set guidelines. Water bodies that are entirely lost
            will be created at the closest possible location; wells,
            ponds, tube-wells, and bore wells lost will be replaced; oil
            and grese traps will prevent contamination due to road
            surface runoff; and water quality will be monitored at
            several locations along the alignment during the operational
            phase. Culverts will maintain the natural drainage of the
            area; and service roads will be provided with lined drains.
            To prevent dust, locate asphalt and batching plants in the
            downwind direction away form human settlements; cover
            vehicles; spray water on earthworks; fit the hot mix plant
            with cyclone/scrubber to control emissions; and control
            exhaust gas emissions by conforming with pollution emission
            levels. Fit vehicles and equipment with exhaust silencers
            and check regularly; restrict schedules construction
            activity; and provide suitable noise barriers or
            double-glazing of windows. Trees will be restored according
            to principles laid out in the Forest Conservation Act of
            1980. Workers will be instructed to inform supervisors of
            any wild fauna. To prevent traffic accidents, prepare a
            traffic management plan, identify temporary diversion
            routes, erect signboards and barricades to divert traffic,
            and use fencing of chain link type to stop straying of
            animals. Service roads will also divert traffic. When
            invaluable cultural property is discovered, construction
            work will be stopped and the Uttar Pradesh Archaeology
            Directorate will be informed.'}

abstracts:
{'cdata!': "The development objective of the
            Integrated Disease Surveillance Project is to improve the
            information available to government health services, and
            private health care providers, on a set of high-priority
            diseases, and risk factors, with a view to improving the
            grassroots responses to such diseases, and risk factors. The
            project four components will: 1) establish and operate a
            central-level disease surveillance unit, under the Ministry
            of Health and Family Welfare (MOHFW) to help coordinate, and
            decentralize disease surveillance activities, and, thus
            complement the states' disease surveillance efforts.
            This component will address constraints due to lack of
            coordination, and update diseases' incidence, through
            appropriate processes, and institutional arrangements at the
            central level; 2) integrate and strengthen disease
            surveillance at the state and district levels, addressing
            coordination constraints at the sub-national levels, the
            limited use of modern technology and data management
            techniques, and, the need to include stakeholder
            participation, including communities' involvement, and
            the private sector; 3) improve laboratory support, upgrading
            laboratories at the state level, to improve laboratory
            surveillance activities. Support includes diagnosis,
            monitoring drug resistance, and changes in disease agents.
            In addition, a quality assurance system for assessing, and
            improving the quality of laboratory data will be introduced;
            and, 4) provide training for disease surveillance and
            action, to support the changes envisaged under the first
            three components, a coordinated training effort to reorient
            health staff towards an integrated surveillance system, and
            provide the new skills needed. Training programs will
            include representatives from the private sector,
            nongovernmental organizations, and community groups."}

display_title: India - Integrated Disease             Surveillance Project : Environmental Assessment
abstracts:
{'cdata!': 'The Integrated Disease Surveillance
            Project for India will strengthen the backbone of
            information network for effective public health delivery
            system in the country, with the objective to improve
            diagnostic facilities in public health laboratories. There
            will be anticipated impacts, and mitigation measures.
            Disease Surveillance Laboratories carry out testing for
            infectious and contagious diseases, such as malaria,
            typhoid, cholera and hepatitis, tuberculosis and HIV/AIDS.
            These laboratories therefore generate waste which includes
            infected human tissues and blood samples, microbes,
            discarded chemicals, sharps, etc. Such waste, if not managed
            properly, carries the risk of infection for waste handlers
            and to the larger community, and is also a potential
            environmental hazard, through pollution of land, water and
            ground water. Although the amounts of waste generated from
            such laboratories is small, its varied and hazardous
            composition requires comprehensive management of the waste
            lifecycle, from source to disposal, to prevent adverse
            impacts on the environment and public health. Adequate waste
            management in laboratories will not only improve overall
            environmental performance but also facilitate in providing a
            safe workplace for the laboratory personnel. In addition,
            laboratories have to comply with the environmental
            regulations of the Government of India. Standard Operating
            Procedures (SOP) for Laboratories will address safety and
            waste management issues. Under the project, operations
            manuals have already been prepared which focus on, among
            other technical topics, good laboratory practices,
            decontamination and Bio-safety issues. A waste management
            program will also be formulated to define the processes
            required for dissemination and implementation at laboratory
            levels and for monitoring. The SOP and waste management
            program will be finalized through a consultative process,
            involving the directors and operators of the national-owned
            and private laboratories to ensure a feasible and pragmatic program.'}

abstracts:
{'cdata!': 'The Integrated Disease Surveillance
            Project shall establish a state-based system of disease
            prevention and control, for timely and effective public
            health actions, responsive to health challenges country
            wide. Tribal populations in India account for significant
            numbers, and it is expected their integration as project
            beneficiaries will positively impact on their health status.
            For this purpose, this Indigenous Peoples Plan (IPP)
            establishes the framework to ensure active involvement of
            tribal groups, in a culturally-compatible manner as follows.
            In particular, focal social mobilization efforts within
            tribal areas should enhance a tribal community
            participation, to be supported by training assistance, and
            awareness generation, information that should be coordinated
            with health staff. Consequently, health staff will
            facilitate working relations with tribal groups, in order to
            design, and use culturally-compatible materials, in
            consultation with, and acceptable to them. Furthermore, the
            development of monitoring and evaluation, based on data
            disaggregated by tribal status, and gender would allow
            tracking the efficacy of the project among tribal groups.'}

{'cdata!': 'The development objective of the Madhya
            Pradesh Water Sector Project (MPWSRP) for India is to
            improve productivity of water for sustainable growth and
            poverty reduction in selected focus river basins (Chambal,
            Sindh, Betwa, Ken and Tons) of Madhya Pradesh. The project
            became effective in January 2005, and with this loan closing
            date extension the total implementation period will be over
            ten years. None of the components has advanced sufficiently

            irrigation schemes through simplified implementation
            arrangements. The project development objective (PDO)

            indicators have been simplified and refined, taking into
            account the revised scope of the components. There will also
            be no change in cost. The total International Bank for
            Reconstruction and Development (IBRD) loan remains US$387.4
            million, of which almost half has been disbursed, while
            there are many firm commitments under ongoing civil works contracts.'}

abstracts:
{'cdata!': 'The Madhya Pradesh Water Sector
            Restructuring Project for India aims to improve productivity
            of water for sustainable growth, and poverty reduction in
            selected focus river basins (Chambal, Sindh, Betwa, Ken and
            Tons) of Madhya Pradesh. The project has the following four
            components: Component 1) will support the establishment and
            operationalization of the proposed planning, allocation and
            regulatory institutions and instruments at the state and
            basin-levels. Component 2) will support measures related to
            delivering reliable irrigation services at rationalized cost
            by financially viable entities. Component 3) will
            operationalize the concepts and provide the necessary
            investments in five basins (Chambal, Sindh, Betwa, Ken, and
            Tons) for (i) reliable delivery of water measured and
            supplied on an appropriate volumetric basis in the
            irrigation systems of these basins to improve system
            performance, cost recovery and accountability of the service
            provider; (ii) an outcome-oriented approach with integrated
            sustainable agricultural intensification and
            diversification; and (iii) improved operation and management
            of the irrigation and drainage schemes. Component 4) The
            project activities would be coordinated by a
            multi-disciplinary Project Implementation Coordination Unit
            (PICU). Support would be provided to assist the PICU with
            its role in facilitating and guiding the implementation and
            monitoring of all project activities, ensuring synergy and
            coordination amongst activities and agencies implementing
            these activities, preparing consolidated reports and
            facilitating training.'}

abstracts:
{'cdata!': "A holistic and integrated vision for
            water development is planned under the Madhya Pradesh Water
            Sector Restructuring Project, to achieve a demand-driven
            process. Although the physical investments will be primarily
            of rehabilitation, an environmental category A
            classification has been adopted, given the spatial scale of
            investments, new nature of some activities, and a number of
            Bank safeguards policies that could be triggered. This
            environmental assessment compiles and reviews baseline data,
            and discusses potential environmental adversity, focused on
            villages covered in household surveys, and those results
            from consultations with stakeholders. Findings suggest a
            mismatch between water availability and demand; uneven and
            unplanned water demand; improper exploitation of
            groundwater; declining quality of water in some basins; and,
            lack of accurate hydrologic data and analysis. In addition,
            physical assets are found to be degraded, institutional
            framework is weak, as is the financial status, aggravated by
            poor irrigated agriculture. Mitigation measures call for:
            strengthening the institutional framework, through periodic
            staff performance evaluation, and training provision,
            particularly in basin management, to achieve optimum
            utilization at State Water Data centers, with linkages with
            the Central Government. A dam safety plan should be
            established, that includes protection of cultural heritage
            sites. Irrigation and drainage systems' operation and
            maintenance practices should be conducted, with regular
            interaction with farmers and users, supported by intensive
            extension programs at the village level. A pest management
            plan should be in place, enhanced by public awareness
            campaigns, and training as needed. Regular soil and land
            inspections should minimize soil erosion, and groundwater
            contamination. The report briefly covers social aspects,
            i.e., tribal development, gender issues, and resettlement."}

display_title: India - Madhya Pradesh Water             Sector Restructuring Project : environmental assessment             executive summary
abstracts:
{'cdata!': 'The Madhya Pradesh Water Sector
            Restructuring Project plans a holistic development, with an
            integrated vision for water sector development and
            management, and user participation in planning, and
            management to achieve a demand driven process. The strategy
            emphasis is on an environmentally, and socially sustainable
            basin approach for water resources planning, and management,
            including conjunctive use of water. The primary objective of
            this environmental impact assessment is to identify key
            environmental, and social issues related to the project, for
            the compilation of the base line data, based on household
            and village surveys, and consultations with stakeholders.
            Thus, identified key issues include a mismatch between water
            availability & demand; uneven and unplanned water
            demand; improper exploitation of ground water; poor quality
            of water; lack of accurate and consistent hydrologic data
            & analysis; and, weak Institutional framework, as well
            as weak irrigated agriculture. Upon a screening and
            selection criteria, interventions and detailed design for
            implementation would be strengthened by a periodic
            performance evaluation. Training and capacity building
            should ensure environmental and social issues are
            appropriately addressed. Among the mitigation measures, a
            general condition of dams and appurtenant works should be
            established, based on available data and identified distress
            situation. On the basis of this comprehensive assessment,
            and identification of potential distress problems, periodic
            visits, and field inspections should be conducted. A
            hydrological review should include flood routing studies,
            seasonal gate operation procedures, and examining the
            existing surplus arrangements. Furthermore, a structural
            review should consider the instruments and devices, critical
            structural elements of the dam, conducting stability
            analysis, etc. Regarding investigations and designs,
            necessary surveys, should be conducted, to plan remedial
            measures, and propose structural/non-structural operational
            procedures for safety of the dam. In addition, technical
            training should be provided, addressing pest management
            issues, ensured by adequate monitoring. Securing fisheries
            development should include ways to increase seed production
            in the state, management of various water bodies, safeguards
            for the fishermen and community, and monitoring of the
            interventions, and associated impacts. The report also
            addresses social, tribal, and resettlement issues.'}

display_title: India - Maharashtra Rural Water             Supply and Sanitation Project : indigenous peoples plan
abstracts:
{'cdata!': "The Second Rural Water Supply and
            Environmental Sanitation Project for Maharashtra, India will
            safeguard the tribals' interest in scheduled areas. The
            tribal development plan will have two major objectives: i)
            one related to rural water supply and sanitation delivery
            being attempted through fostering, and empowering
            autonomous, inclusive, equitable and accountable grassroots
            tribal institutions, and ii) institutional strengthening to
            enable the state government in general. The concept of
            self-help and community sharing or resources is ingrained in
            the tribal culture; involving local communities in
            decision-making is part of the tradition. Key issues are
            discussed and conflicts, if any, are resolved in the
            presence of hereditary village head and other elders. The
            project's strategy of decentralization of Village
            Panchayats, and user groups, fits in with the tribal
            socio-economic characteristics and cultural value. At the
            same time, a study on traditional systems of governance
            among tribals will also be completed during the first year
            of the project, with a view to identify
            culturally-appropriate ways of local governance and hence to
            improve tribals' participation and inclusion. The
            tribal development strategy will also be premised on the
            Community Demand Driven (CDD) principles of: autonomy,
            subsidiary, self selection and demand driven participation,
            inclusion and equity, transparency and accountability, and
            cost sharing. Tribals mobilized into groups will be
            capacitated to plan, implement and operate and maintain the
            project activities/facilities."}

{'cdata!': 'The assessment of outcome is

            following. Research and experience suggest that reform
            programs are more likely to succeed when owned, and designed

            Although this entails higher administrative costs for the
            Bank, the process supports the required incentive mechanism,
            and, facilitates an exit strategy for the Bank, if the
            reform program falters. For example in this case, a
            follow-up adjustment operation will be based on the
            continuation of the reform program. However the pace of
            progress of different components of a government-owned
            reform program varies, thus it is important to determine the
            critical elements of the program, where progress is needed,
            and how would the pace sustain the credibility of the
            overall program; i.e., in Andhra Pradesh, unless the
            financial performance of the power sector is improved on a
            sustained basis, the fiscal reform will remain tentative. A
            possibility could have been to agree on specific actions
            that would have helped improve the power sector financial
            performance. Finally, it is highlighted that partnerships,

{'cdata!': "The project development objective is to

            policy, and institutional changes, as well as capacity

            implementation of community-based forest management, while
            project management support will be provided, to include
            monitoring and evaluation, consulting services and studies,
            and operational costs; 2) forest management, focused on

            improved planning, and silvicultural practices, using
            multiple shrub and tree species, including medicinal plants,
            agro-forestry, common land afforestation, and fodder and
            pasture development. Adaptive forestry research will also be
            supported, as will the preparation of a forestry inventory,
            an environmental and pest management plan, and a forest
            management information system; and, 3) community
            development, to improve village infrastructure, and
            livelihoods, through forest, and non-forest based income
            generation activities. A tribal development plan would be an
            integral sub-component in preparing investment proposals,
            and, a resettlement plan would include mitigation measures
            for adverse impacts."}

display_title: India - Andhra Pradesh Community             Forest Management Project : social assessment
abstracts:
{'cdata!': 'The Andhra Pradesh Forest Community
            Project aims to reduce rural poverty through improved forest
            management with community participation. In 1992 the
            government adopted a Joint Forest Management approach,
            wherein all forest dependents organize themselves into a
            cohesive group - Van Samrakshana Samithies (VSS) - to
            protect, regenerate, and manage the forests. From a mere 200
            VSSs in 1995, today there are more than 6,700 VSSs in the
            state managing 1.68 million hectares of forest area. A
            comprehensive and integrated Social and Environmental
            Assessment has been done wherein to key issues for forestry
            sector in general and for the project in particular. Some of
            the issues include: a) Forestry and environment improvement
            can directly influence the poverty problem to a great
            extent. The challenge is how to reach the poorest of the
            poorest. b) Rapport with the stakeholders by Forest
            Department builds up the trust relationship. c) Establishing
            and maintaining backward linkages as well as integrating
            gender concerns for overall development of rural and tribal
            families can be better done in a group rather than an
            individual. d) Combined trainings, orientations,
            deliberations, filed exposures, and workshops are found to
            be quite effective tools for advocacy, capacity building,
            social mobilization, improving performance and skills of
            VSS, NGOs, and functionaries or facilitators. e) Integration
            of micro-plan with other development plans would go a long
            way to be effective.'}

display_title: India - Andhra Pradesh Community             Forest Management Project : environmental assessment :             Environmental management plan
abstracts:
{'cdata!': 'This environmental assessment of the
            Andhra Pradesh Community Forest Management Project
            anticpates the following negative impacts and describes
            measures to mitigate them. The measures avoid loss of
            biodiversity, soil erosion, degradation of vegetation, and
            reduced agricultural productivity by encouraging short
            rotation species with higher sustained yields and incomes,
            using a watershed approach for soil and water conservation,
            environmental education, and conducting research. Also, the
            plan raises fuelwood plantations to meet demand for
            firewood, popularize alternate energy systems, augment
            fodder resources, upgrade cattle population. To prevent
            excessive use of pesticides and fertilizers, it employs
            integrated pest management; enhances use of organic
            techniques; conducts awareness, training, and capacity
            building programs; launches studies; and conducts monitoring
            and evaluation. To promote personal hygiene and avoid poor
            sanitation, it encourages local traditions, periodic health
            check-ups and vaccinations; supplies smokeless and fuel
            efficient chulhas, biogas plants, solar lanterns, and clean
            and safe drinking water facilities; and composts through
            traditional methods and vermin composting. Finally, to
            advance forest conservation, minimum desired clearing and
            cleaning measures will be undertaken, soil conservation
            measures will be used to avoid soil erosion, mixed
            plantations will be used, and only species tolerating
            salinity and alkalinity will be planted.'}

abstracts:
{'cdata!': 'This Tribal Development Strategy and
            Action Plan for the Andhra Pradesh Community Forest
            Management Project aims to reduce the dependence of tribals
            on the forests for their economic subsistence and to narrow
            the gap in the levels of development of tribal and
            non-tribal through deliberate actions for socioeconomic
            development of tribals. The strategy will ensure tribal
            inclusion in the entire process of preparation,
            implementation, and monitoring of project activities. It
            will ensure that the benefits of the project are available
            to tribals more than or at least at par with the rest of the
            community. It should provide a base for tribals in the
            project area to receive adequate developmental attention.
            Given the socioeconomic backwardness of scheduled tribes,
            tribals and their areas continue to lag behind the general
            population. The approach so far adopted is the top down
            planning and implementation as a result tribal communities
            could not benefit from the various constitutional
            safeguards, policy regulations, and government development
            programs. This demonstrates the need for focused attentions
            on tribal issues and involving them in the planning of
            activities included under Vana Samrakshana Samithies based
            Tribal Development Plans. There is a need to plan and
            implement deliberate interventions under the Project. At the
            same time, there is a need to dove tail the on-going
            government development schemes to ensure sustainability.'}

            intense debate. This paper combines a randomized control
            trial of a citizenship training and facilitation program in
            rural India, with an in-depth, four-year ethnography of the
            intervention to understand the underlying mechanisms of
            change. The quantitative data show no impact from the
            intervention. Household and village survey data from 100
            treatment and 100 control villages show considerable
            improvement across a wide variety of governance and
            participation indicators over time, but the differences in
            the changes between treatment and control villages are not
            statistically significant. The detailed qualitative data
            from a 10 percent subsample allow us to unpack the reasons
            why the intervention "failed," highlighting the
            role of variations in the quality of facilitation, lack of
            top-down support, and difficulties with confronting the
            stubborn challenge of persistent inequality. However, the
            qualitative investigation also uncovered subtle treatment
            effects that are difficult to observe in structured surveys.
            The paper thus demonstrates that a concerted effort to use
            "thick description" to uncover the process of
            change using careful and detailed qualitative work can add
            value to standard impact evaluations.'}

abstracts:
{'cdata!': "The Andhra Pradesh Rural Poverty
            Reduction Project development objective is to enable the
            rural poor, particularly the poorest of the poor, in Andhra
            Pradesh to improve their livelihoods and quality of life.
            The project supports the Government of Andhra Pradesh's
            ongoing long-term Rural Poverty Reduction Program, which
            aims to eradicate poverty; promote human capital
            development; focus on the welfare of children, particularly
            girls, women, the old, and the infirm; and build an
            equitable society in which people participate in making
            decisions which affect their lives and livelihoods. The
            project components are: 1) institution and human capital
            development; 2) establishing of the Community Investment
            Fund (CIF) designed to transfer financial and technical
            resources to Community Based Organizations (CBOs) and local
            governments to support subprojects in a) social development,
            b) community-level infrastructure, c) income-generation and
            livelihood improvements, and c) land purchases and
            development, and water resource management; 3) support to
            pilot programs; 4) educational support for out-of-school
            children and dropouts; 5) support to persons with
            disabilities; and 6) support activities for project
            management to the main implementing agency, SERP. The
            project strongly contributes to the Bank's Country
            Assistance Strategy (CAS) objectives and main goal, to
            assist the pro-poor rural development sector."}

abstracts:
{'cdata!': "The focus of the Andhra Pradesh Rural
            Poverty Reduction Project is to improve opportunities for
            rural poor in meeting priority, socioeconomic needs. Given
            that tribal population constitutes the poorest, and most
            vulnerable of the social groups in the project area, this
            Tribal Development Plan, or Indigenous Peoples Plan, is
            proposed as an integral part of the project, in accordance
            with the Bank's Operational Directive. The plan looks
            at the status of tribal groups, or scheduled tribes, on key
            development indicators, presents the methodology for its
            development, and reviews the legal, and institutional
            framework for protection of tribal rights. Based on
            participatory initiatives, and consultations with scheduled
            tribes, the plan aims at fostering full respect for dignity,
            human rights, and cultural uniqueness of indigenous peoples,
            while ensuring they do not suffer adverse effects due to the
            development process, but rather benefit economically, in a
            culturally and socially compatible manner. Mitigation will
            seek to provide technical guidance by the concerned line
            departments, ensuring training assistance to institutional
            personnel, and tribal leaders, to consolidate institutional
            interventions. Measures to minimize adversity stipulate:
            provision of training in soil conservation, and land
            development activities, including in dry land farming
            techniques, and watershed management; organization of
            demonstration plots, and seed production sites, including
            training for a balanced use of fertilizers, and pesticides,
            bio-fertilizers, and the use of improved seeds; provision of
            fund support for land development, and purchase of
            agro-inputs and/or irrigation schemes; training provision in
            post-harvest practices, processing and preservation of
            horticulture produce, in addition to marketing commodities
            training; training provision to traditional medicine men,
            and assistance to procure herbal medicines, with provision
            of market linkages; training on techniques to support tribal
            handicrafts, and market linkages; identification of
            unemployed tribal youth, to impart training on self
            employment schemes, or job opportunities, with provisions
            from institutional support; and, establishment of grain
            banks, and rice credit aimed as food security management."}

display_title: India - Andhra Pradesh Rural             Poverty Reduction Project : environmental assessment (Vol.             4) : Proceedings of public consultations on environment             management plan and pest management plan
abstracts:
{'cdata!': 'The Andhra Pradesh Rural Poverty
            Reduction Project will enable the poorest people to
            articulate their needs in accessing and influencing the
            quality of basic services, and in creating their own
            opportunities to improve their living standards. To this
            end, subprojects will cover the areas of livestock
            development, minor irrigation, agriculture development,
            forest products, construction, and micro enterprises. Based
            on the scale, and nature of subprojects, the screening of
            this environmental management framework (EMF) is categorized
            within levels 0-3, dependent on the environmental magnitude.
            Measures to mitigate environmental adversity include: fodder
            cultivation, and management (crop residue) to minimize
            reduced grass productivity; regulated grazing to control
            soil erosion; composting practices, and use of manure, thus
            prevent organic waste; maintenance of a minimum distance of
            200 meters between bore wells to mitigate decline of water
            in existing open wells, or bore wells; groundwater
            recharging practices, and surface water harvesting -
            including efficient irrigation, and soil moisture
            conservation methods - in addition to re-planting low
            water-demanding crops, and/or horticulture adoption, to
            prevent depletion of groundwater; use of silt on farmland to
            enhance soil fertility, including afforestation; optimal
            application of fertilizers, and organic fertilizers, with
            minimal applications of pesticides, to avoid water
            pollution; use of energy efficient, and environmentally
            sound building construction materials; appropriate waste
            disposal, and management of solid, and liquid wastes to
            control organic pollution.'}

abstracts:
{'cdata!': 'This environmental assessment for the
            Andhra Pradesh Urban Reforms and Municipal Services Project
            anticipates negative environmental impacts and proposes
            measures to mitigate them. To get a better understanding of
            the social and environmental adverse impacts that may arise
            due to developmental intervention, especially infrastructure
            improvements in urban areas, the study team selected 10
            sub-projects either completed, under implementation, or
            proposed in the towns selected for the study. Identified as
            expected types of losses are: loss of land, built up
            property, productive assets, livelihood, public utility
            lines, access to urban civic services, and cultural
            properties. The report points out the special
            vulnerabilities to historically disadvantaged groups like
            certain castes, tribes or indigenous populations, the
            physically handicapped, women-headed households, children,
            the elderly, and low-income groups. Possible environmental
            impacts include flooding, water logging, changes in land
            fertility, loss of flora and fauna, changes in the water
            table, erosion, land pollution, changes in air temperature,
            acidic rain, air quality changes due to dust and smoke, odor
            nuisance, changes in noise levels due to traffic congestion
            and dumping, impacts on aquatic life, decreased oxygen,
            over-exploitation and contamination of groundwater, clogged
            surface drains from refuse and sediments, waste spills,
            wetland loss, leaching from solid waste, health risks caused
            by infection from organic waste, and health risks due to
            infected animals, among others.'}

display_title: India - Andhra Pradesh Urban             Reforms and Municipal Services Project : environmental             assessment (Vol. 2) : Social and environmental assessment
abstracts:
{'cdata!': 'The objective of the Andhra Pradesh
            Urban Reforms and Municipal Services Project for India is to
            support urban reforms to improve city management and upgrade
            and expand municipal services through provision of physical
            infrastructure with particular focus on reducing urban
            poverty. Negative measures include: flooding, water logging,
            changes in land fertility, loss of flora and fauna, changes
            in the water table, erosion, land pollution, changes in air
            temperature, acidic rain, air quality changes due to dust
            and smoke, odor nuisance, changes in noise levels due to
            traffic congestion and dumping, impacts on aquatic life,
            decreased oxygen, over-exploitation and contamination of
            groundwater, clogged surface drains from refuse and
            sediments, waste spills, wetland loss, leaching from solid
            waste, health risks caused by infection from organic waste,
            and health risks due to infected animals, among others.
            Mitigation measures include: a) the ground water abstraction
            should be restricted to permissible limit. Ground water
            balance must be taken in to consideration while using
            groundwater as a source; b) care shall be taken to avoid
            creation of borrow pits as far as possible, if not, proper
            care shall be taken for human and animal safety and to avoid
            water logging; c)  all pipe appurtenances should be tested
            before laying; d) future traffic projections to decide on
            the carriageway, proper identification of material dumping
            during construction; and e) check for noise levels of
            construction equipment construction activities with moderate
            to high noise levels should be carried out as far as
            possible only during daytime.'}

India - Grand Trunk Road             Improvement Project
abstracts:
{'cdata!': "The World Bank has adopted a
            programmatic approach to support the Government of
            India'a National Highway Development Program (NHDP)
            through a series of loans. The Grand Trunk Road Improvment
            Project (GTRIP) is the second project in the series,
            following the Third National Highway Project (TNHP), which
            was approved and is under implementation. The development
            objectives of GTRIP are consistent with those of the TNHP:
            1) to reduce transport constraints on national economic
            activity; and 2) to improve institutional capabilities to
            manage road programs, assets, and services on a more
            commercial basis. There are three project components. The
            first finances highway upgrading, including civil works for
            widening and strengthening highway lanes, supervision
            consultant services, as well as funding land acquisition,
            utility relocation, resettlement and rehabilitation,and
            environmental mitigation/management. The second component
            finances road safety and corridor management works,
            including consultant services for a safety audit, a program
            of road improvements specifically targeted at supporting
            improved methods for reducing accidents and improving safety
            on the national highway network, and a program of
            maintenance works to introduce alternative contracting
            methods and to strengthen maintenance management practices.
            The third component establishes a public-private partnership
            in road concession, and the fourth component supports social
            and environmental as well as road capacity building."}

display_title: India - Grand Trunk Road Project             - environmental assessment (Vol. 18) : Follow-up public             consultation programme
abstracts:
{'cdata!': 'The Grand Trunk Road Project will
            improve the high traffic volumes traversing the Ganges
            Plains at the Agra-Barwa Adda corridor through the
            construction and expansion of roads and highways. However,
            project implementation will adversely impact the
            environment, causing air pollution (particularly endangering
            cultural heritage sites, i.e., the Taj Mahal), water
            pollution, and major crop losses. During the
            pre-construction and construction stages, measures to
            minimize adversity shall include clearance of the
            right-of-way, transplanting pre-identified trees, and
            replacing/relocating utilities likely to impact the
            livelihoods of the neighboring population. Debris shall be
            disposed of by the contractor at selected dump sites;
            topsoil shall be stockpiled to restore disturbed areas, and
            borrow pits shall be dug at road embankments. To prevent
            soil erosion, sedimentation, and water pollution, the use of
            dikes, sediment basins, and slope drains shall be used in
            accordance with engineering designs. Lubricants and oil
            spills shall be contained through oil interceptors for
            refueling cases with fuel storage at appropriate sites, and
            disposal of petroleum products in accordance with
            environmental guidelines. Spoils, and solid wastes shall be
            treated, and disposed of at selected disposal sites. Silt
            fencing and retention ponds will be installed to prevent
            water pollution and groundwater depletion.'}

India - Grand Trunk Road Project             - resettlement action plan
abstracts:
{'cdata!': 'The Grand Trunk Road Project involves
            the construction, and expansion of roads and highways,
            traversing both agricultural, and urban areas. The existing
            right-of-way (ROW) in urban areas is limited, not adequate
            to accommodate road widening, thus realignment will require
            additional width of the ROW; while, along the agricultural
            belts, most of the roadside land is privately owned;
            consequently, land acquisition will take place, displacing a
            number of squatters within the public ROW, and affect as
            well, families in agricultural areas. This resettlement
            action plan (RAP) aims to minimize reallocation, and improve
            living standards, or at least maintain the livelihoods of
            affected people. To minimize losses, concentric road
            widening, and raised carriageways shall be adopted along
            built-up stretches of the corridor, or as possible, only
            one-side expansion shall be performed, and, bypasses are
            proposed around major urban centers. Based on socioeconomic,
            and census data, and consultations with stakeholders,
            resettlement measures shall include: loss of land,
            buildings, or other assets, including crop losses,
            compensated at replacement costs, or through cash
            compensation for land valued at prevailing market prices;
            and, new job opportunities, and training will be provided as
            needed. Although land compensation will not be provided to
            encroachers, and squatters, compensation for structures, and
            lost assets shall be paid at replacement costs to those who
            belong to vulnerable groups. The Grievance Redressal
            Committee shall assist with resettlement claims.'}

{'cdata!': 'The project development objective of the
            Karnataka Community Based Tank Management Project is to
            improve rural livelihoods and reduce poverty by developing
            and strengthening community-based approaches to improving
            and managing selected tank systems. The project adopts a
            programmatic approach to community-based tank management and
            covers the first phase of this program--2000 tanks of the
            estimated 37,000 minor irrigation tanks in the state 0r
            72,000 ha of the 685,000 ha (11 percent) of the estimated
            command area irrigated by tanks. The project consists of
            three components: 1) establishing an enabling environment
            for the sustainable, decentralized management of tank
            systems; 2) strengthening community-based institutions to
            assume responsibility for tank system development and
            management; and 3) undertaking tank system improvements. The
            third component is further sub-divided into: a) improving
            the operational performance of selected tank systems through
            a menu of physical interventions identified and executed by
            local users and b) facilitating technical training and
            on-farm demonstrations in water management, agriculture, and
            horticulture development, fisheries, forestry, and fodder
            production to help ensure that improved water storage and
            efficiency is translated into increased household incomes.'}

abstracts:
{'cdata!': "As defined by the Constitution of India
            - not just confined to the concept of indigenous peoples
            (IP) - the term IP shall comprise scheduled castes (SCs),
            and scheduled tribes (STs), i.e., groups categorized as not
            being in the mainstream economy. The social assessment
            process covered the project area of some fifty tanks, and
            focused on issues relating to tribal, and vulnerable groups.
            It identified that SCs, and STs tend to be socially, and
            economically marginalized, dependent on dominant castes, and
            communities. This Indigenous Peoples Plan (IPP), based on
            the social assessment, reviewed in addition the legislation
            safeguarding those groups, and, in consultation with
            affected members, determined mitigation measures as follows.
            Due to the high incidence of landlessness, and in order to
            strengthen off-farm, and non-farm occupations, Tanker Users
            Groups' activities should be oriented for inclusion of
            SCs, and STs, to promote animal husbandry, and, encourage
            the development, and marketing of dairy products. Moreover,
            the promotion of irrigation should expand through the
            participation of communities, in renovating the open wells
            belonging to SCs, and STs, and, facilitating improved
            agricultural practices supported by the line Departments,
            and research institutes, including the supply of seeds,
            fertilizers, and technical know-how. Similarly, access to
            institutional credit should be facilitated, and linkages
            with the agricultural marketing network established.

            and, an integrated mass education and literacy programs

display_title: India - Karnataka Community Based             Tank Management Project : resettlement action plan
abstracts:
{'cdata!': 'The main objective of the Karnataka
            Community Based Tank Management Project is to strengthen
            community-based approaches to managing selected tank systems
            in Karnataka. The tank system is a common property natural
            resource, critical to user groups for equitable distribution
            of benefits. Whereas land acquisition, and physical
            displacement issues are expected to be minimal, this
            resettlement action plan (RAP) addresses mainly the
            encroachment issue, surrounding the tank system,
            particularly in tank bed areas, since project interventions
            will likely affect adversely on people who will lose the
            encroached land. Based on social assessments, and profiles
            of such population, the approach proposed to be adopted is
            on the basis of a voluntary surrender of land, within the
            provisions of the Land Acquisition Act, which provide
            adequate legal, and policy framework to mitigate adversity
            on the local population. The entitlement framework provides
            for land losses (both owned or encroached), physical
            structures, and asset losses, including livelihood losses.
            Losses will be compensated at replacement costs, according
            to market values, in cash, or land-for-land compensation,
            whereas vulnerable groups, and people living on encroached
            land, will be assisted, if land encroached is more than 20
            percent of operational holdings, either through
            land-for-land compensation as available, and/or through
            skills training, or a productive asset grant. Assistance
            will be provided to access institutional credit; and, skills
            training will be provided for income generating activities,
            or crop production. Food security will be safeguarded by
            providing assistance during the transitional period, for the
            initial three years. Consultations with the affected
            community will be conducted, to monitor the agreed
            assistance provisions for lost, or diminished livelihood,
            while grievance mechanisms will also be available.'}

display_title: India - Karnataka Community Based             Tank Management Project : environmental assessment : Summary             report (advanced draft)
abstracts:
{'cdata!': 'This environmental assessment (EA) for
            the Karnataka Community Based Tank Management Project,
            combined different methods for the purpose of data
            gathering, and consultations to understand the
            environmental, and social implications of the project. It
            looks at the major problems faced by the tank system,
            namely, siltation of tank resulting in storage capacity
            reductions, encroachment on natural, and other water ways,
            and feeder channels in the catchment area, extension of
            cultivation and encroachment in the foreshore area, damages
            to tank embankments, surplus weirs, and, main and field
            channels. Mitigation measures are as follows. Project
            activities would coordinate with the Watershed Department to
            ensure the sustainable management of the tank catchments are
            carried out to prevent land degradation, and, appropriate
            sub-basins would be used as a framework to coordinate
            interventions. Desiltation of tanks should be done based on
            technical topographic, hydrologic, and engineering studies,
            and, the creation of adequate dead storage areas should
            reduce evaporation, while damaged sluice will be
            rehabilitated to ensure tank safety. A detailed policy, and
            plan framework have been developed to address the issue of
            encroachment of tank bed from the foreshore area. Tank User
            Groups would identify rehabilitation activities on damaged
            main, and field channels, while water-logging will be
            monitored by the community. The use of organic manure should
            be a part of the agricultural diversification extension
            services. While desiltation may be beneficial on falling
            groundwater levels, automatic water level recorders would be
            installed to monitor groundwater extraction, and ensure
            equitable distribution of water. Based on community
            consultations, the report also addresses social impacts, and
            resettlement issues, and as well, a pest management plan
            consistent with integrated management is included.'}

display_title: India - Karnataka : financing             education in the context of economic restructuring
abstracts:
{'cdata!': "The study addresses four major concerns
            within the Bank's Economic Restructuring Program in
            Karnataka: 1) identifying the priority issues facing the
            education sector; 2) indicating possible areas for
            expenditure reform, to improve the efficiency, and equity of
            public spending in education; 3) identifying measures to
            strengthen the effectiveness of public expenditure; and, 4)
            assessing the resource requirements for school education.
            The report reviews achievements, and educational trends in
            the nineties, looking at the factors shaping
            Karnataka's education development, to then examine
            public expenditures on education, and the efficiency of
            public spending. Improvements in the effectiveness of public
            expenditures in education are proposed, namely in the input
            utilization of teachers, and non-teachers; in management
            strengthening of the private sector; and, decentralization
            in the education system. To attain the elementary, and
            secondary education goals, considerable financial
            allocations will be required, where the volume of additional
            requirements depends critically on the strategies adopted by
            the Government of Karnataka (GOK), particularly as these
            affect the expenditures on teachers. The analyses show that
            if the GOK adopts fiscally sustainable strategies in school
            education, provided fiscal reforms are successful, financing
            requirements for the educational system expansion of higher
            quality, could be met, mainly from its own resources, and
            private sector mobilization, as well as from the adoption of
            cost-reducing strategies to narrow the financing gap."}

abstracts:
{'cdata!': "This is a resettlement plan for the
            Karnataka State Highways Improvement Project. The
            resettlement policy addresses the direct and indirect
            impacts of project construction and operation on affected
            persons, families, households, communities, and groups. The
            most direct and immediate impacts are those associated with
            project construction, mainly land acquisition. Other losses
            include loss of shelter, and other assets within the
            project's corridor of impact as well as roadside
            structure, business establishments, and public facilities.
            Mitigation is provided through compensation and assistance
            to project-affected persons. These social units are entitled
            to compensation and assistance on the basis of this policy
            framework adopted by the project. Mitigation is provided for
            loss of assets, including land and house or workplace; loss
            of livelihood or income opportunities and collective impacts
            on groups, such as loss of community assets, common property
            resources, and others. The people likely to be affected by
            loss of assets and livelihood will be surveyed and
            registered, and project monitoring and evaluation will
            compare long-term impact against baseline socio-economic
            data. Mitigation and support mechanisms for those affected
            by collective impacts are collectively-oriented, and these
            efforts will be monitored to examine the impacts and
            benefits for the groups involved."}

display_title: India - Karnataka State Highways             Improvement Project : environmental assessment (Vol. 13) :             EIA and EMP summary (revised) for phase II Bijapur By-pass
abstracts:
{'cdata!': 'This is an environmental assessment for
            the Karnataka State Improvement Project which upgrades
            roads, identifies negative environmental impacts and
            proposes measures to mitigate them. Impacts from location
            include changes in gravity flow irrigation, a rise in the
            water table, extensive deforestation, and improper road
            drainage systems. To mitigate these impacts, raise the
            height of roads to prevent contamination, establish deep cut
            drains, pave the shoulders to keep them free from vegetative
            growth, and restrain truckers from overloading. Impacts due
            to road design will be alleviated as follows: to arrest
            traffic pollution, absorb noise, and provide an alternative
            fuel source, trees will be replanted on roadsides. During
            construction borrow pits will be restored and dressed to
            create a slope consistent with the level of adjoining land.
            Maintaining earthen drains and limiting construction
            activities for bridges and culverts to the dry season will
            help reduce soil quality deterioration and the resulting
            water pollution. Disposing of solid and liquid wastes, and
            stream courses and drainage will help maintain water
            quality. To control dust, asphalt and hot mix plants will be
            located away from inhabited areas; trucks will be covered;
            and machinery and equipment will be maintained. During the
            operational phase, emission checks will reduce pollution,
            planting will help prevent surface run-off, and accidents
            involving hazardous cargo will be offset by an emergency
            response system.'}

abstracts:
{'cdata!': 'The Karnataka State Highways Improvement
            Project for India aims to improve the core road network in
            Karnataka. The core road network is defined here as the
            state highways plus the most heavily trafficked major
            district roads. The project will produce the following
            outputs: It will enhance the capacity and quality of the
            core state highway network; provide safer transit on
            selected corridors; improve allocation and provide adequate
            funding for the road sector; and provide more efficient and
            effective network management and delivery of road
            infrastructure services. The project has four components: 1)
            upgrading and widening about 1000 km of priority state
            roads; 2) rehabilitating about 1300 km of state roads; 3)
            supporting the implementation of the Institutional
            Development Action Plan for the Public Works Department,
            pre-investment studies and other miscellaneous expenses
            including incremental operating costs; and 4) supporting a
            pilot safety program. The project finances civil works for
            road construction and rehabilitation; consultancies for
            advisory services, training, construction supervision,
            project management, system development and implementation;
            equipment and logistical syupport; as well as required
            social rehabilitation and resettleemnt, and environmental
            mitigation measures. The estimated costs for physical works
            include the base cost, supervision, land acquisition, social
            resettlement and rehabilitation, and physical and price contingencies.'}

abstracts:
{'cdata!': "This is a resettlement plan for the

            include loss of shelter, and other assets within the
            project's corridor of impact as well as roadside
            structure, business establishments, and public facilities.

            to project-affected persons. These social units are entitled

            framework adopted by the project. Mitigation is provided for

            resources, and others. The people likely to be affected by

            compare long-term impact against baseline socio-economic
            data. Mitigation and support mechanisms for those affected
            by collective impacts are collectively-oriented, and these
            efforts will be monitored to examine the impacts and
            benefits for the groups involved."}

display_title: India - Karnataka State Highways             Improvement Project : environmental assessment : Sectoral             environmental assessment report
abstracts:
{'cdata!': 'This is an environmental assessment for
            the Karnataka State Improvement Project which upgrades
            roads, identifies negative environmental impacts and
            proposes measures to mitigate them. Impacts from location
            include changes in gravity flow irrigation, a rise in the
            water table, extensive deforestation, and improper road
            drainage systems. To mitigate these impacts, raise the
            height of roads to prevent contamination, establish deep cut
            drains, pave the shoulders to keep them free from vegetative
            growth, and restrain truckers from overloading. Impacts due
            to road design will be alleviated as follows: to arrest
            traffic pollution, absorb noise, and provide an alternative
            fuel source, trees will be replanted on roadsides. During
            construction borrow pits will be restored and dressed to
            create a slope consistent with the level of adjoining land.
            Maintaining earthen drains and limiting construction
            activities for bridges and culverts to the dry season will
            help reduce soil quality deterioration and the resulting
            water pollution. Disposing of solid and liquid wastes, and
            stream courses and drainage will help maintain water
            quality. To control dust, asphalt and hot mix plants will be
            located away from inhabited areas; trucks will be covered;
            and machinery and equipment will be maintained. During the
            operational phase, emission checks will reduce pollution,
            planting will help prevent surface run-off, and accidents
            involving hazardous cargo will be offset by an emergency
            response system.'}
