display_title: India - Current economic position             and prospects
abstracts:
{'cdata!': 'The report, Current Economic Position
            and Prospects of India was prepared in July 1958, and was
            the result of an earlier mission to India in May and June of
            1958. It follows on from a memorandum on recent economic
            developments, which was circulated at the beginning of April
            1958 (Report No.AS-66a) Prior to that, the last economic
            report on India was circulated in April 1957 (No, AS-60a).
            The Bank mission last visited India in the summer of 1956
            and prepared a comprehensive report (AS-54a). India is in
            the grips of a foreign exchange crisis. Earlier this year it
            looked as if the pressure on foreign exchange reserves might
            at last be easing off, but since the middle of March the
            situation has another turn for the worse. The large numbers
            of imports, especially capital goods, has been the principal
            reason for the crisis, coupled with an increase in defense
            spending, especially in paying for orders with overseas
            defense contractors. The Indian government is attempting to
            address this with its second Five-Year plan, but the
            situation has left the government little if any room to
            maneuver. There is a real risk therefore that before long
            India will be faced with a choice between cutting back
            industrial production for lack of raw materials, leaving
            resources tied up in un completed projects and deferring
            some of the payments due for imports. In practice, all three
            of these things might have to be done to some extent to
            alleviate the crisis.'}

display_title: India - Memorandum on recent             economic developments
abstracts:
{'cdata!': 'The memorandum, Recent Economic
            Developments in India, was prepared in April 1958 and was
            meant to supplement reports AS-60a, dated May 1957 and
            AS-54a dated 1956. The memorandum states that India has
            achieved a pace of rapid acceleration in the pace of her
            economic development in the last two years. The development
            and increased defense expenditures have resulted in a huge
            increase in demand for domestic supplies. This has resulted
            in a major increase in imports. This has caused a deficit
            which India has partially covered by foreign aid, but she
            has also been forced to draw down her foreign exchange
            reserves substantially. While agricultural production has
            gone on to record levels, industrial production has begun to
            flatten out. The bank was confident that inflationary
            pressures could be avoided, if taxes could be reduced and
            domestic demand satisfied, but this is not expected to be an
            easy process by any means.'}

display_title: India - Current economic position             and prospects
abstracts:
{'cdata!': 'The report, Current Economic Position
            and Prospects of India was compiled in May 1957. This report
            was meant to supplement the last report from a bank mission
            to India (AS-54a, dated September 1956). The report
            concludes that during the first year of the Second Five-Year
            Plan India has got into serious balance of payments
            difficulties by trying to do too much at once.  A 25 percent
            increase in public development expenditures has been
            accompanied by an unexpected boom in private industrial
            investment, defense expenditures have been stepped up, and
            it can be assumed that there has been some increase in
            personal consumption with higher incomes generated by
            development. Industrial production has risen sharply, but
            there has been no corresponding expansion in agriculture,
            and real output as a whole has not grown fast enough to keep
            pace with the overall rise in demand. This has left a gap to
            be filled by additional imports, which have had to be paid
            for by drawing heavily on foreign exchange reserves. The
            Mission is satisfied from its talks in New Delhi that
            serious, if belated, efforts are now being made to put the
            balance of payments right and to curb investment
            expenditures. Commercial imports have been sharply
            restricted from the beginning of 1957; a six-month
            development holiday has been declared for all new projects,
            except where special arrangements can be made for external
            financing; and possible future commitments for both public
            and private sectors are being thoroughly screened. All these
            measures will help to restrain demand for consumption and
            investment and they must inevitably result in time in some
            slowing down of the pace of development. But it will be
            several months before their full impact is felt on the
            balance of payments because of the heavy foreign exchange
            commitments previously incurred.'}

display_title: India - Current economic position             and prospects
abstracts:
{'cdata!': 'The report, Current Economic Position
            and Prospects of India was prepared in August 1956, and was
            the result of an earlier mission to India. The report aimed
            to examine the economic growth of India as she instituted
            the second of her five year plans to marshal the resources
            of her 385 million people and see what the implications
            would be in terms of India\x92s balance of payments and also on
            her ability to borrow abroad to finance her development. The
            report sought to avoid appraising events from a solely
            Western perspective and to gain a measure of historical
            perspective as well. The report pointedly reminds the reader
            that it was created some nine years after India gained
            independence, and the effects of partition were still very
            present. The general conclusion from the mission\x92s report
            was that, so long as close and continuous attention is given
            to the development of exports, India should be able to
            service a considerably higher debt than at present both in
            dollar and nondollar currencies. She has enjoyed a surplus
            on dollar account for some time and her membership of the
            sterling area gives her considerable flexibility. It is
            likely, however, that the majority of the purchases made
            with proceeds of additional foreign borrowing will he made
            in non-dollar countries which are often able to supply
            capital equipment on more reasonable terms than the United
            States. It would be natural therefore that a substantial
            part of any additional borrowing by India should be in
            non-dollar currencies, at least to the extent that such
            currencies are available for lending.'}

display_title: Postwar economic growth in             Southeast Asia
abstracts:
{'cdata!': "The purpose of this paper to review the
            major trends in the development of Southeast Asia since the
            war and to appraise the areas conditions and growth
            prospects. The survey covers Burma, Ceylon, India,
            Indonesia, Malaya, Pakistan and Thailand. It did not appear
            useful to discuss the development in the Associated States
            of Indochina since the largest part of the country was a
            battlefield until recently. The gravity of the traditional
            development problem in Southeast Asia can probably be best
            described in terns of three factors: 'ow per capita
            income, the lack of drive in a largely self-subsistent
            society, and high pressure of population on land. The static
            character of the economy, associated with a low level of
            savings and investment, prevents the creation of sufficient
            employment opportunities outsides agriculture to absorb both
            the steady increment to the labor force and the existing
            rural population surplus.As a result, aggregate saviors in
            the industrial sector remain low. This in turn prevents an
            increase in the rate of accumulation of industrial capital,
            while new capital formation in agriculture is directly
            limited by the low level of per capita agricultural
            income.Since the war, two external factors have tended to
            break down the tendency towards stagnation inherent in the
            economies of the area. The first and most important of these
            was the achievement of political independence.The second
            dynamic factor working from the outsize was the sharp
            fluctuation world demand caused by the Korean war.In the
            future, the development efforts may be expected not only to
            continue, but to increase. They will be greatly facilitated
            if the capital-output ratio (capital requirements per unit
            of additional output) is maintained at the low level of
            2.0-25:1 which has thus far prevailed, While development
            prospects appear particularly promising in India, all
            indications are that other countries in Southeast Asia will
            also continue to regard economic growth as the central
            problem of their public policy."}

display_title: India - Current economic position             and prospects
abstracts:
{'cdata!': 'This report, Current Economic Position
            and Prospects of India, was prepared in November 1954. The
            report concludes that the economic situation is development
            with stability. Though there have been increases in
            development expenditures, there has been no corresponding
            inflationary pressure. There also has been very little
            deficit financing.  The deficit is expected to shrink as the
            Indian budget usually does better than expected. Foreign
            assistance authorized during the period March 1951 to July
            1954 and undrawn portions of IBRD loans sanctioned prior to
            1951/52 together amount to Rs. 2,342 millions. In the first
            three years of the Five Year Plan, Rs. 1,319 millions of
            this amount was utilized. During the current year the
            estimates of likely utilization are placed at Rs. 318
            millions. IBRD loans negotiated since 1951/52 amount to Rs.
            199 million. There has also been a corresponding decrease in
            the price index and a increase in agricultural production.
            Industrial production has also been on the increase. This
            has resulted in a balance of payments surplus. Thus the
            implementation of the Five Year Plan has been carried out
            under conditions of financial stability, growing
            agricultural and industrial production and without balance
            of payments difficulties.'}

display_title: India - Industrial finance corporation
abstracts:
{'cdata!': 'The report, Industrial Finance
            Corporation of India, was prepared in December 1952. The
            object of this paper is to describe the purposes, capital
            structure and operations of the Industrial Finance
            Corporation (IFC) of India. Unfortunately, the capital
            market had entered into a prolonged period of shortage from
            which it has not yet emerged. Several reasons have been
            given for the stagnation in the capital market. The release
            of a large backlog of demand after the war, high taxation,
            the redistribution of income in favor of lower income groups
            with less developed habits of saving and investment, the
            hoarding of idle funds and durables partly as a result of
            tax evasion, and the wariness of investors at the prospect
            of government interference, have been some of the economic
            factors in the situation. The IFC was established by a
            special act of Parliament in 1948 for the purpose of making
            medium and long term credits more readily available to
            industrial concerns India in cases where normal bank
            accommodation would be inappropriate or recourse to capital
            issue methods might be impracticable. The IFC is now in its
            fifth year of operation and is firmly established with the
            strong backing of Government. It has a good reputation in
            business and industrial circles in India. Its Board consists
            of men with long experience of banking and industry in
            India. Its financial position has improved steadily during
            the past four years and the volume of business done has
            expanded. The changes made by the Amendment Act should serve
            to expand the scope of IFC1s operations and to strengthen
            its finances. With the aid of Bank loans the IFC should make
            an increasing contribution to the expansion of industrial
            and private enterprise on which the development plans of
            India depend upon.'}

abstracts:
{'cdata!': "This report covers the period from

            Bank mission visited India to obtain a first-hand impression
            of the economic and financial situation and to make an
            initial survey of such development projects as the
            Government might put forward tor consideration. Formal loan
            negotiations were opened in June 1949. In February 1950 a
            small Bank mission visited India to report on economic
            developments, the economic relations between India and
            Pakistan, and India's capacity to service further
            dollar loans. The third and latest loan agreement, for a
            loan of $18.5 million, was signed in April 1950 to finance
            the Bokaro-Konar project, forming part of the first phase of

display_title: Recent economic and financial             developments in India
abstracts:
{'cdata!': 'The recent financial and economic
            situation in India can be characterized as a period of
            disinflation which started in the late autumn of 1951.
            Inflationary pressure has persisted in India ever since the
            war and it was increased as a result of the post-Korean
            boom. India followed a cheap money policy in the postwar
            period which included support of the government bond market
            by the Reserve Bank. Since 1950, however, the Reserve Bank
            has altered its policy, first, by allowing a gradual fall in
            government bond prices. The wholesale price index which
            reached a high of 462 in the middle of April 1951 began to
            decline moderately in the second half of 1951 and reached
            433.1 on the December average. The substantial price decline
            in the first months of 1952 was accompanied by an increased
            supply of commodities. Thus the market situation has changed
            allover India. The most surprising change took place in the
            food position.'}

display_title: The agriculture development of             India with special reference to the first-five plan
abstracts:
{'cdata!': 'The purpose of this report is to
            appraise the agricultural aspects of the first five-year
            plan. The present Indian price control policy, which is
            expected to be adhered to, in general, during the period of
            the plan, has attempted to keep agricultural prices from
            rising. For the achievement of the targets, in the case of
            cash crops, major reliance is placed on private initiative
            through the price incentive. In the case of cereals major
            reliance is laid on government sponsored and administered
            schemes for irrigation, land reclamation and clearance,
            increased use of fertilizer, better seed and an expanded
            extension service. Here the price incentive, in general, is
            a subordinate factor. The methods adopted to develop Indian
            agriculture from a long term point of view are sound but the
            results, in the form of expanded output of cereals, are
            likely fully to accrue more slowly than is expected.'}

display_title: Review of recent economic and             financial developments in India
abstracts:
{'cdata!': "A review of India's economic and
            financial situation in 1949 and in the first months of 1950
            indicates some manifestations of improvement and increased
            stability, but proper account must be taken of those factors
            which have injected a substantial degree of uncertainty into
            India's economic outlook. Favorable developments in the
            Indian economic situation during the past year are: (1)
            foreign trade and balance of payments; (2) domestic
            production; and (3) price movements. The most significant
            developments on the unfavorable side of the recent economic
            situation are as follows: (1) the budget position; (2) the
            capital market; and (3) India- Pakistan relations. In mining
            and manufacturing an increase of production took place in
            most fields. India's railway transport facilities
            showed a marked improvement in 1949, virtually eliminating
            the post war transportation bottleneck and permitting the
            removal of priorities on freight shipments. Attempts have
            been made to promote sales of Government of India Treasury
            Deposit receipts. For 1949, internal prices in India
            remained relatively stable in spite of some fluctuations
            during the year and divergence in price movements among
            commodity groups. India's balance of trade showed a
            marked improvement after June 1949, following the heavy
            trade deficits that were incurred in the last half of 1948
            and especially in the first half of 1949. The import surplus
            was sharply reduced in the third quarter of 1949 and an
            export surplus was achieved in the fourth quarter of 1949
            and the first quarter of 1950."}

display_title: Summary of economic and financial             developments in India in the last half of 1949
abstracts:
{'cdata!': "The purpose of the present study is to
            review briefly the economic and financial developments in
            India in the latter half of 1949. The heavy trade deficit,
            incurred in the first half of 1949 was sharply reduced in
            the second half of the year and India's sterling
            balances which fell by about Rs. 2,000 million during
            January-June, remained approximately constant between June
            and December. Devaluation of the rupee by 30 percent in
            September was followed by an increase in Indian export
            volume, as well as value in terms of rupees, while imports
            were sharply curbed in the latter months of 1949 by severe
            administrative restrictions. In spite of the reduction in
            the trade deficit, relative stability was maintained in the
            internal money supply and in the price level. The most
            disturbing aspect of recent developments in India, has been
            the virtually complete stalemate in trade relations with
            Pakistan. A serious burden is imposed on India's
            internal finances by heavy military outlays which are
            associated in large part with the deterioration in
            Indo-Pakistan relations. Cabinet officials state only that
            the payments deficit for the year ending in June 1950 will
            be kept within the amount of the releases from India's
            sterling balances during this period. This, however, will
            represent a substantial improvement over the extreme
            imbalance in India's external accounts which developed
            during the last half of 1948 and the first six months of 1949."}

display_title: India's creditworthiness
abstracts:
{'cdata!': "This report discusses India as a credit
            risk. The service of domestic debt accounts for about 12-1/2
            percent of its ordinary expenditure. Except for the dollar
            obligation to the International Monetary Fund, India has
            practically no foreign debt. On the other hand, it owes
            substantial sterling balances of nearly $2,900 million).
            When the preset extraordinary expenditures on national
            defense, on food subsidies and on refugees decline, India
            should be able not only to reduce its high rate of taxation,
            but even to provide a surplus for development financing. If
            present anti-inflationary policy continues and no unexpected
            difficulties interfere,  a further lessening of inflationary
            pressure may be expected since no net purchasing power is
            being generated by monetary authorities. The restoration of
            confidence is a prerequisite to an improvement of the
            capital market. Only then will capital be available for the
            investment needed to increase production in India. The
            Government is alive to this and is trueing steps to create a
            more favorable business climate.  An increase of available
            savings should supplement public expenditures on development
            projects. It is expected that the overall food deficit would
            be reduced and that the country may be able to obtain larger
            food imports from prewar sources or other parts of the soft
            currency area. Such a change in the food import and
            production situation would alone substantially lessen the
            gravity of the dollar problem. However, the country must
            continue to purchase more in soft currency areas and at the
            same time sell more in the hard currency area. To do the
            latter, the problem of competitive prices must be solved in
            order to strengthen and restore the position of Indian goods
            in foreign markets. In assessing India's
            creditworthiness, account must be taken of its sterling
            balances, and especially of the prospects of the U.K. to
            allow India to draw on these balances for purchases within
            the sterling area and to provide her with a modest yearly
            allocation in dollars."}

display_title: The banking system of India -             appendix to summary study of India
abstracts:
{'cdata!': 'Banking in India may be divided into two
            categories : the organized banking system and indigenous
            banking. Organized banking is of relatively recent origin
            and is essentially a Western import rather than an outgrowth
            of domestic financial and credit institutions. Indigenous
            banking, on the other hand, is probably as ancient as
            commerce itself. Organized banking consists of (a) the
            Reserve Bank of India; (b) the so-called Scheduled Banks,
            (c) the Non-Scheduled Bank composed primarily of the smaller
            joint-stock banks incorporated under the Indian Companies
            Act of 1913; and (d) special types of banking and savings
            institutions. Indigenous banking comprises a large and
            heterogenous group of individuals and partnerships
            throughout India (also called shroffs) engaged in lending
            money, dealing in internal bills, and accepting deposits.
            The role of different types of banking institutions varies
            with respect to different monetary and financial aspects of
            the Indian economy. Indigenous banking predominates in
            internal financing.'}
